<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
Let~$s$ and~$r$ be two positive integers such that~$s \geq r$.
An $r \times r$ matrix $B=(b_{ij})$ with integer entries is called
\emph{skew-symmetrizable} if $d_i b_{ij} = -d_j b_{ji}$
for some positive integers $d_1, \dots, d_r$.
In other words, a matrix is skew-symmetrizable if it differs from a
skew-symmetric matrix by a rescaling of its rows by positive scalars.
	An $s \times r$ integer matrix $\tilde{B}$,
 whose top $r\times r$ submatrix is
skew-symmetrizable is called an \emph{extended skew-symmetrizable} matrix.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
If $\tilde{B}$ is an $s \times r$ integer matrix whose top $r \times r$ submatrix $B$ is 
skew-symmetric, then we say that $\tilde{B}$ \emph{comes from a quiver}, because $B$
is the adjacency matrix of a quiver $Q$ on $r$ \emph{mutable vertices} $v_1,\dots, v_r$ 
with $b_{ij}$ arrows from 
$v_i$ to $v_j$ for each positive entry $b_{ij}$.  Moreover, we can encode the bottom
$(s-r) \times r$ submatrix of $\tilde{B}$ by adding $(s-r)$ \emph{frozen vertices}
$v_{r+1},\dots, v_s$, where for $r+1 \leq i \leq s$, we have $b_{ij}$ arrows from 
$v_i$ to $v_j$ if $b_{ij}$ is positive, and we have $-b_{ij}$ arrows from
	$v_j$ to $v_i$ if $b_{ij}$ is negative.  The resulting quiver $\tilde{Q}$ is sometimes called an \emph{ice quiver}.
By convention  there are no arrows connecting two frozen vertices.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:matrix-mutation}
Let $\tilde{B} =(b_{ij})$ be an $s \times r$
extended skew-symmetrizable integer matrix.
For $1 \leq k \leq r$, the
\emph{matrix mutation $\mu_k$ in direction~$k$} transforms
$\tilde{B}$ into the $s \times r$ matrix $\mu_k(\tilde{B}) = (b'_{ij})$ whose
entries are given by:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:matrix-mutation1}
b'_{ij} =
\begin{cases}
-b_{ij} & \text{if $i=k$ or $j=k$;} \\[.05in]
b_{ij}+b_{ik}b_{kj} & \text{if $b_{ik}>0$ and $b_{kj}>0$;}\\[.05in]
b_{ij}-b_{ik}b_{kj} & \text{if $b_{ik}<0$ and $b_{kj}<0$;}\\[.05in]
b_{ij} & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:seed}
Let~$s$ and~$r$ be two positive integers such that~$s \geq r$, and 
let $\mathcal{F}$ be a field 
	isomorphic to the field of rational functions over~$\mathbb{Q}$ (alternatively, over $\mathbb{C}$)
in $s$ independent variables.
A \emph{labeled seed} $\Sigma$ in $\mathcal{F}$ is a pair
$\Sigma:=(\tilde \mathbf{x}, \tilde B)$~where
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=.15in]
\item $\tilde \mathbf{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_s)$ is an $s$-tuple of
elements of~$\mathcal{F}$ forming a
\emph{free generating set}; that is, $x_1, \dots, x_s$
are algebraically independent, and $\mathcal{F} = \mathbb{Q}(x_1, \dots, x_s)$;
\item $\tilde B=(b_{ij})$ is an $s \times r$ extended
  skew-symmetrizable integer matrix.
\end{itemize}
We use the following terminology:
$\tilde \mathbf{x}$ is the (labeled)
\emph{extended cluster}
of the labeled seed $(\tilde \mathbf{x}, \tilde B)$;
the $r$-tuple~$\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_r)$ is the (labeled)
\emph{cluster}
of this seed;
the elements $x_1, \dots, x_r$ are its \emph{cluster variables};
the remaining elements $x_{r+1}, \dots, x_s$ of $\tilde \mathbf{x}$ are the
\emph{frozen variables} (or \emph{coefficient variables});
the matrix~$\tilde B$ is the \emph{extended exchange matrix} of the seed;
its top $r\times r$ submatrix~$B$ is the \emph{exchange matrix}.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:seed-mutation}
Let $(\tilde \mathbf{x}, \tilde B)$ be a labeled seed, and let 
 $k\in\{1,\dots,r\}$.
The \emph{seed mutation} $\mu_k$ in direction~$k$
transforms
$(\tilde \mathbf{x}, \tilde B)$ into the new labeled seed
$\mu_k(\tilde \mathbf{x}, \tilde B) = (\tilde \mathbf{x}', \tilde B')$
defined as follows:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=.15in]
\item
$\tilde B'= \mu_k(\tilde B)$
as in \cref{def:matrix-mutation}.
\item
	the extended cluster $\tilde \mathbf{x}' = \mu_k(x_1,\dots,x_s):=(x_1',\dots,x_s')$ is
given by $x_j'=x_j$ for~$j\neq k$,
where $x'_k \in \mathcal{F}$ is determined
by the \emph{exchange relation}
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:exch-rel-geom}
x_k \, x'_k = \prod_{b_{ik}>0} x_i^{b_{ik}}
+ \prod_{b_{ik}<0} x_i^{-b_{ik}}.
\end{equation}
\vspace{-10pt}
\end{itemize}
If the indexing set for one of the two monomials above is the empty
set, then by convention we set the corresponding product equal to~$1$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:cluster-algebra}
Let $\Sigma = (\tilde \mathbf{x}, \tilde B)$ be a labeled seed as above, and let 
$\mathcal{X}$ be the set of all cluster variables
that we can obtain by performing any sequence
of mutations starting at $\Sigma$.

We let the \emph{ground ring} be $R = \mathbb{C}[x_{r+1}, \dots, x_{s}]$,
the polynomial ring generated by the frozen variables.
(A~common alternative is to take $R = \mathbb{Q}[x_{r+1}^{\pm 1}, \dots, x_{s}^{\pm 1}]$,
the ring of Laurent polynomials in the frozen variables.)
	The \emph{cluster algebra}~$\mathcal{A}:=\mathcal{A}(\Sigma)$ (over~$R$)
is the $R$-subalgebra of the ambient field~$\mathcal{F}$
generated by all cluster variables: $\mathcal{A}= R[\mathcal{X}]$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:clustervariety}
An \emph{affine cluster variety} is the 
	variety
$V:=\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{A}$, where $\mathcal{A}$ is a cluster algebra which is finitely generated.
Each cluster $\mathbf{x}$ for $\mathcal{A}$ can be thought of as coordinates of an open 
	torus ${(\mathbb{C}^*)}^s \subset V$  called a \emph{cluster chart} or \emph{cluster torus}.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The cluster variety agrees with the union of cluster tori up to codimension
$2$.
Fock and Goncharov~\cite{FG} 
gave an alternative definition
of \emph{cluster $A$-variety} (also called \emph{cluster manifold})
as the scheme consisting of 
the algebraic tori corresponding to seeds of $\mathcal{A}$ glued along 
birational maps corresponding to mutations.  This cluster manifold
can be identified with the union of all cluster tori in $\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{A}$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:gradedexchange}
Let $(G,+)$ be an abelian group. Choose positive integers $r \leq s$, and let $\Upsilon = (\tilde{B}, (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s))$, where $\tilde{B}=(b_{ij})$ is an $s \times r$ exchange matrix, and $\sigma = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s) \in G^s$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{gradedseed}
	\sum_{i=1}^s b_{ij} \sigma_i = 0 \hspace{1cm} \text{ for all }1 \leq j \leq r, \qquad \text{ i.e. }\sigma \tilde{B}=0.
\end{equation}
We then call $\Upsilon$ a \emph{$G$-balanced exchange matrix}, or that 
	$\Upsilon$ is \emph{$G$-balanced}.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:quiver}
	Let $\Upsilon = (Q,(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s))$, where $Q$ is a quiver on vertices $v_1,\dots,v_s$, and $(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s)\in G^s$. For $v_i$ a mutable vertex of $Q$, let 
	\[
		\operatorname{in}_{\sigma}^{Q}(v_i) = \sum_{v_j \to v_i} \sigma_j
		\hspace{.5cm} 
		\text{ and }
		\hspace{.5cm} 
		\operatorname{out}_{\sigma}^{Q}(v_i) = \sum_{v_i \to v_j} \sigma_j,
	\]
	where the first sum is over all arrows in $Q$ entering $v_i$,and the second sum is over all arrows in $Q$ leaving $v_i$. We say that $\Upsilon$  is \emph{$G$-balanced} at the mutable vertex $v_i$ if  
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:grading}
		\operatorname{in}_{\sigma}^Q(v_i) = \operatorname{out}_{\sigma}^Q(v_i).
	\end{equation} 
	We say that $\Upsilon$  is a \emph{$G$-balanced quiver} if it is $G$-balanced at every mutable vertex.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:balancepropagates} 
	Note that if~\eqref{gradedseed} holds, then we have that 
\begin{equation}\label{newgrading0}
	\left( \sum_{b_{ik}>0} b_{ik} \sigma_i \right)- \sigma_k = 
	\left( \sum_{b_{ik}<0} -b_{ik} \sigma_i \right) - \sigma_k.
\end{equation}
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{def:Gmutation}
	Let $(G,+)$ be an abelian group, and let $\Upsilon = (\tilde{B}, (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s))$ be a $G$-balanced exchange matrix as above. For $k\in [1,r]$, we define the mutation $\mu_k(\Upsilon)$ of $\Upsilon$ by $\mu_k(\tilde{B}, (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s)):= (\mu_k(\tilde{B}), (\sigma'_1,\dots,\sigma'_s))$, where 
	\[
		\sigma'_i :=\begin{cases}  
			\left( \sum_{b_{ik}>0} b_{ik} \sigma_i \right)- \sigma_k & \text{ if }i=k \\
			\sigma_i & \text{ otherwise.}
		\end{cases}
	\]
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:propagate}
If $\Upsilon$ is a $G$-balanced exchange matrix, then for 
any mutable direction $k$, we have that 
$\mu_k(\Upsilon)$ is a $G$-balanced exchange matrix.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Suppose that~\eqref{gradedseed} holds. We need to check that after we mutate in direction $k$,~\eqref{gradedseed} still holds for $\mu_k(\Upsilon)$. Let $\tilde{B}'=(b'_{ij}):=\mu_k(\tilde{B})$.

	We first verify that~\eqref{gradedseed} holds when $j=k$. By the definition of mutation, the $k$th column of $\tilde{B}'$ is the negative of the $k$th column of $\tilde{B}$, and $b'_{kk} = 0$. Thus
	\[
		\sum_{i=1}^s b'_{ik} \sigma'_i = \sum_{i=1}^s (-b_{ik}) \sigma_i = 0.
	\]


	Now fix $j$ and suppose that $b_{kj}>0$ (the case where $b_{kj}<0$ is analogous). Then we have 
	\begin{align*}
		\sum_{i=1}^s b'_{ij} \sigma'_i &=
		\sum_{i=1, i\neq k}^s b'_{ij} \sigma_i + b'_{kj} \sigma'_k\\
		&= \sum_{i=1, i\neq k}^s b'_{ij} \sigma_i + 
		(-b_{kj})\left[ \left(\sum_{b_{ik}>0} b_{ik} \sigma_i \right) - \sigma_k \right] \\
		&= \sum_{i \text{ where } b_{ik}>0} (b_{ij} + b_{ik} b_{kj}) \sigma_i 
		+ \sum_{i \text{ where } b_{ik}<0} b_{ij} \sigma_i 
		- b_{kj} \left(\sum_{b_{ik}>0} b_{ik} \sigma_i \right)
		+ b_{kj} \sigma_k
		\\
		&= \sum_{b_{ik}>0} b_{ik} b_{kj} \sigma_i - 
		b_{kj} \left( \sum_{b_{ik}>0} b_{ik} \sigma_i \right) = 0,
	\end{align*}
	as desired. Finally, fix $j$ where $b_{kj}=0$. Then $b'_{ij}=b_{ij}$ for all $i$, and in particular $b'_{kj}=b_{kj}=0$, so 
	\[
		\sum_{i=1}^s b'_{ij} \sigma'_i = \sum_{i=1}^s b_{ij} \sigma_i = 0.
	\]
	This completes the proof that $\mu_k(\Upsilon)$ is a graded seed.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:lamspeyercohomology}
	Let $((x_1,\dots,x_s),\tilde{B})$ be any seed of $\mathcal{A}$.
	An element of $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal{A})$ is determined by its action on 
	$(x_1,\dots,x_s)$.  Given $(\zeta_1,\dots,\zeta_s)\in {(\mathbb{C}^*)}^s$, there
	is an automorphism $\phi$ with $\phi(x_i) =\zeta_i x_i$ if and only if 
	$\zeta \in \ker(\tilde{B}^t)$.\footnote{We interpret this kernel multiplicatively.}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{def:gradedseed}
Let $\Upsilon = (\tilde{B}, (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s))$ be a $G$-balanced
exchange matrix as in~\cref{def:gradedexchange}, and 
suppose that $\Sigma = (\tilde{B}, (x_1,\dots,x_s))$ is a seed with the same
$s \times r$ exchange
matrix $\tilde{B}$.
We then call the triple
	$(\tilde{B}, (x_1,\dots,x_s), (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s))$ a 
\emph{$G$-graded seed}.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:gradingpropagates} 
	Let $(\tilde{B}, (x_1,\dots,x_s), (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s))$ be a {$G$-graded seed}. Let $\sigma(x_i):= \sigma_i$ for $1\leq i \leq s$ be a grading on the initial cluster variables. Since~\eqref{gradedseed} holds, when we mutate in direction $k$, we obtain 
	\[
		x'_k = \frac{\prod_{b_{ik}>0} x_i^{b_{ik}} + \prod_{b_{ik}<0} x_i^{-b_{ik}}}{x_k},
	\]
	and we have a well-defined grading on the new cluster variable $x'_k$, namely
	\begin{equation}\label{newgrading}
		\sigma(x'_k) := 
		\left( \sum_{b_{ik}>0} b_{ik} \sigma_i \right)- \sigma_k = 
		\left( \sum_{b_{ik}<0} -b_{ik} \sigma_i \right) - \sigma_k.
	\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{def:gradedclustervariable}
	Let $(\tilde{B}, (x_1,\dots,x_s), (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s))$ be a {$G$-graded seed} as in \cref{def:gradedseed}. We refer to  the assignment $\sigma(x_i):=\sigma_i$ as the \emph{$G$-grading} on the initial cluster variables.
	Then~\eqref{newgrading} gives rise to a well-defined grading
	\[
		\sigma: \mathcal{X} \to G
	\]
	on all cluster variables.
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
Let $(G, +)$ be an abelian group, and let $\widetilde{B} = (b_{ij})$ be an $s \times r$ exchange matrix. We denote $\mathfrak{gr}(\mathcal{A}(\widetilde{B}), G)$ as the group of $G$-gradings on $\widetilde{B}$.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
In forthcoming work, Burcoff et al.~\cite{enumeration_signed_seeds} enumerate the number of $G$-gradings in the case $G = \mathbb{Z} / p \mathbb{Z}$ for $p$ prime. They prove that if $B$ has full rank over $\mathbb{F}_p$, then there are $p^{\text{\# frozen}}$ $\mathbb{Z}/p \mathbb{Z}$-gradings.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a cluster algebra with a torus action giving a $\mathbb{Z}^n$-grading $\sigma_{\text{std}} \in \mathfrak{gr}(\mathcal{A}, \mathbb{Z}^n)$. For any abelian groups $G$ and $H$, the following diagram commutes 
\[
	\begin{tikzcd}
		{{(G \oplus H)}^{\oplus n}} & {G^{\oplus n} \oplus H^{\oplus n}} \\
		{\mathfrak{gr}(\mathcal{A}, G \oplus H)} & {\mathfrak{gr}(\mathcal{A}, G) \oplus \mathfrak{gr}(\mathcal{A}, H)}
		\arrow["\cong", from=1-1, to=1-2]
		\arrow["{\Psi_{G \oplus H}}", from=1-1, to=2-1]
		\arrow["{\Psi_G \oplus \Psi_H}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
		\arrow["{\cong }", from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\end{tikzcd}
\]
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\cite[Definition 3.1 and Proposition 6.1]{ca4}\label{prop:g}
Let $B$ be an $n \times n$ exchange matrix,
and let $\tilde{B}$ be a $2n \times n$ exchange matrix,
whose principal (i.e., top $n \times n$) part is $B$
and whose complementary (i.e., bottom) part is the $n \times n$ identity matrix.
Let $G = \mathbb{Z}^n$, and let $\mathbf{e}_1,\dots, \mathbf{e}_n$ denote the standard
basis vectors of $\mathbb{Z}^n$.
	Let $\Upsilon:=(\tilde{B}, (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{2n}))$, where
$\sigma_i:=\mathbf{e}_i$ for $1 \leq i \leq n$,
and $\sigma_{j+n} = -\mathbf{b}_j$ for $1 \leq j \leq n$,
where $\mathbf{b}_j=\sum_i b_{ij} \mathbf{e}_i$ is the $j$th column of $B$.
Then $\Upsilon$ is a $G$-balanced exchange matrix.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
We just need to check that~\eqref{eq:multi} holds.  In other words, we need to show
that for each $1\leq j \leq n$, we have
$\sigma_1 b_{1j} + \cdots + \sigma_n b_{nj} + \sigma_{n+j} = 0$.
But the left hand side equals 
$b_{1j} \mathbf{e}_1 + \cdots + b_{nj} \mathbf{e}_n - \mathbf{b}_j$,
which equals $0$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
\label{def:signedseed}
	Let $G=\{-1,1\}$ be the abelian group on two elements. Choose positive integers $r \leq s$, and let $\Sigma = (\tilde{B}, (x_1,\dots,x_s))$ be a seed, where $\tilde{B}=(b_{ij})$ is an $s \times r$ exchange matrix, and $(x_1,\dots,x_s)$ is an initial cluster. Let $\tilde{\Sigma}: = (\Sigma, (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s))$, where $\sigma = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s) \in G^s$, and 
	\begin{equation}\label{signedseed}
		\prod_{i=1}^s (\sigma_i)^{b_{ij}} = 1 
		\hspace{1cm} \text{ for all }1 \leq j \leq r.
	\end{equation}
	We then call $\tilde{\Sigma}$ a \emph{signed seed}.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:quiver2}
Consider a seed $\Sigma=(Q,(x_1,\dots,x_s))$ together with 
a tuple $(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s) \in \{-1,1\}^s$.
If $v_i$ is a mutable vertex of $Q$,
let $$\operatorname{in}_{\sigma}^{Q}(v_i) = \prod_{v_j \to v_i} \sigma_j
	\hspace{.5cm} 
	\text{ and }
	\hspace{.5cm} 
\operatorname{out}_{\sigma}^{Q}(v_i) = \prod_{v_i \to v_j} \sigma_j.$$
	Then $({\Sigma},(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s))$  is a {signed seed} if 
for each mutable vertex $v_i$ we have 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:grading2}
	\operatorname{in}_{\sigma}^Q(v_i) = \operatorname{out}_{\sigma}^Q(v_i).
\end{equation}
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:positiveseed}
Suppose that $\sigma_i=1$ for all $1\leq i \leq s$.
Then for any seed $\Sigma$, the pair $(\Sigma, (\sigma_1,\dots, \sigma_s))$
is a signed seed, which gives rise to the constant grading 
$\sigma: \mathcal{X} \to G$ in which $\sigma(x)=1$ for all $x\in \mathcal{X}$.
We call this the \emph{totally positive signed seed}.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
Suppose that $V$ is an affine cluster variety as in \cref{def:clustervariety}. The coordinate ring $\mathbb{C}[V]$ can then be identified with a cluster algebra $\mathcal{A} = \mathcal{A}(\Sigma)$. Let $\mathcal{X}$ be the set of cluster variables of $\mathcal{A}$. Given $v\in V$ and $x\in \mathcal{X}$, we say that the \emph{sign of $x$ on $v$ is $1$} and write $\operatorname{sign}(x(v))=1$ if $x(v)$ is real and strictly positive. Similarly, we say that the \emph{sign of $x$ on $v$ is $-1$} and write $\operatorname{sign}(x(v))=-1$ if $x(v)$ is real and strictly negative.


Given a signed seed $\tilde{\Sigma}$ for $\mathbb{C}[V]$
with grading $\sigma: \mathcal{X} \to \{-1,1\}$, we define the \textit{(open) signed cell} and \textit{(closed) signed cell} to be the following subsets of real points: 
\begin{align}
	V_{>0}^{\sigma} & :=\{v\in V(\mathbb{R}) \ \vert \ \sigma(x)x(v) > 0 \text{ for all }x\in \mathcal{X}\}, \\
	V_{\geq 0}^{\sigma} & := \{v\in V(\mathbb{R}) \ \vert \ \sigma(x) x(v) \geq 0 \text{ for all }x\in \mathcal{X}\}.
\end{align}
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
If $\sigma$ is identically $1$, as in \cref{rem:positiveseed}, then
\begin{equation}
V_{>0}^{\sigma}=\{v\in V \ \vert \ x(v) >0  \text{ for all } x\in \mathcal{X}.\}
\end{equation}
We may denote this signed cell by $V_{>0}$; it is often called the 
\emph{totally positive} part of $V$ \cite{sf-icm}.


If for example $V$ is the set of $n \times n$ matrices and $\mathbb{C}[V]$ is 
endowed with the usual
cluster structure (see \cref{sec:matrices}) then the cluster variables
include all minors of an $n \times n$ matrix, and 
$V_{>0}$ recovers the set of \emph{totally positive matrices}.
If $V$ is the (affine cone over the) Grassmannian 
$\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$ and $\mathbb{C}[\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}]$ is endowed with the usual
cluster structure (see \cref{sec:Grassmannian}) then 
the cluster variables include all Pl\"ucker coordinates, and 
$V_{>0}$ recovers the \emph{totally positive Grassmannian}, that is,
the subset of the Grassmannian where all Pl\"ucker coordinates are positive.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:test}
Let $V$ be an affine cluster variety  whose coordinate ring
can be identified with a cluster algebra $\mathcal{A}$ with cluster variables $\mathcal{X}$. Let $\sigma$ be a grading coming from a signed seed $\tilde{\Sigma}_0$. Then the signed cell $V^{\sigma}_{>0}$ is homeomorphic to an open ball of dimension $s$, where $s$ is the size of any extended cluster.


Moreover, for any signed seed $\tilde{\Sigma}=(\tilde{B}, (x_1,\dots,x_s), 
(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s))$ 
which is mutation equivalent to $\tilde{\Sigma}_0$, we have 
\begin{align}
	V_{>0}^{\sigma}&=\{v\in V(\mathbb{R}) \ \vert \ \sigma(x) x(v) > 0 \text{ for all }x\in \mathcal{X}\} \label{first}\\
	&=\{v\in V(\mathbb{R}) \ \vert \ \sigma(x_i) x_i(v) > 0 \text{ for }1 \leq i \leq s.\} \label{second} 
\end{align}	
In other words, each signed seed provides a finite ``test for membership'' for whether
	a given element $v$ lies in the signed cell $V^{\sigma}_{>0}$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:ball}
If $\Sigma=(\tilde{B},(x_1,\dots,x_s))$ is a seed for the cluster variety $V$ and if $(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s)$ is an arbitrary element of $\{\pm {1}\}^{s}$, then
\[
	V_{>0}^{(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s)} :=\{v\in V(\mathbb{R}) \ \vert \ \sigma_i x_i(v) > 0 \text{ for }1 \leq i \leq s\}
\]
is homeomorphic to $(\mathbb{R}_{>0})^s$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
By the Laurent phenomenon for cluster algebras, if 
the values of the cluster variables
$x_i(v)$ for $1\leq i \leq s$ are fixed and 
nonzero, this uniquely
determines 
the value of $x(v)$ for any $x\in \mathcal{X}$.
Thus 
	$V^{(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s)}_{>0}$
	is homeomorphic to 
$(\mathbb{R}_{>0})^{s}$ via the map 
$$v \mapsto (\pm x_1(v), \dots, \pm x_s(v)),$$
where the sign in front of $x_i(v)$ is given by $\sigma_i$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
We start by proving \eqref{second}.  (We have that \eqref{first} holds
by definition.)
Clearly 
\[
	\{v\in V(\mathbb{R}) \ \vert \ \sigma(x) x(v) > 0 \text{ for all }x\in \mathcal{X}\}  \subseteq \{v\in V \ \vert \ \sigma(x_i)x_i(v) > 0 \text{ for }1 \leq i \leq s.\}.
\]
To show the other inclusion, consider some $v$ such that 
$\operatorname{sign}(x_i(v))=\sigma(x_i) \text{ for }1 \leq i \leq s.$
It is enough to show that if we mutate one step away from $\tilde{\Sigma}$,
obtaining a new cluster variable $x'_k$, we have 
$\operatorname{sign}(x'_k(v)) = \sigma(x'_k)$.


By 
\eqref{eq:exch-rel-geom}
	we have 
\begin{equation*}
	x'_k(v) = 
	\frac{\prod_{b_{ik}>0} x_i(v)^{b_{ik}}
	+ \prod_{b_{ik}<0} x_i(v)^{-b_{ik}}}{x_k(v)},
\end{equation*}
and if we write \eqref{newgrading} multiplicatively, we get 
\begin{equation*}
\sigma(x'_k) := 
	\frac{\prod_{b_{ik}>0} \sigma(x_i)^{b_{ik}}}{\sigma(x_k)} = 
	\frac{\prod_{b_{ik}<0} \sigma(x_i)^{|b_{ik}|}}{\sigma(x_k)}.
\end{equation*} 
In particular the sign of the two monomials
	$\prod_{b_{ik}>0} x_i(v)^{b_{ik}}$ and 
	$\prod_{b_{ik}<0} x_i(v)^{-b_{ik}}$ is equal, and 
	$$\operatorname{sign}(x'_k(v))  = 
	\frac{\prod_{b_{ik}>0} \operatorname{sign}(x_i(v))^{b_{ik}}}{\operatorname{sign}(x_k(v))} = 
	\frac{\prod_{b_{ik}>0} \sigma_i^{b_{ik}}}{\sigma_k}=\sigma(x'_k)$$ as desired.


Now using \eqref{second} and \cref{lem:ball},
	it follows that $V_{>0}^{\sigma}$ is homeomorphic to $(\mathbb{R}_{>0})^s$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
If $\Sigma = (\tilde{B}, (x_1, \ldots, x_s), (\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_s))$ is a signed seed for the cluster variety $V$, then $V_{\geq 0} \cong V_{\geq 0}^{\sigma}$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
From \cref{prop:lamspeyercohomology}, the signs $(\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_s) \in (\mathbb{C}^*)^s$ determines an automorphism of $\mathcal{A}$ where the induced automorphism on $V$ maps $V_{\geq 0}$ homeomorphically onto $V_{\geq 0}^\sigma$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:frozen-leaf}
	Let $Q$ be a quiver and $x \in Q$ a frozen leaf. Let $Q'$ be the quiver where we remove $x$, freeze the neighbor of $x$, and then remove all edges between frozen vertices. Then, the number of $G$-gradings of $Q$ equals the number of $G$-gradings of $Q'$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The procedure for removing a frozen leaf is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:frozenleaf}. Let $y$ be the neighbor of $x$; it is necessarily mutable. Given a $G$-grading of $Q'$ that we want to extend to $Q$, 
there is exactly one element of $G$ we can assign to $x$ so that the 
resulting $G$-grading is $G$-balanced  at $y$. 
Conversely, a $G$-grading on $Q$ gives a $G$-grading on $Q'$. 
These correspondences are inverse, so we have a one-to-one correspondence between the $G$-gradings on $Q$ and the $G$-gradings on $Q'$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:isolated-vertex}
	Let $Q$ be a quiver and $x \in Q$ an isolated vertex. Then,
	\[
		\# \{ \text{$G$-gradings of $Q$} \} = |G| \cdot \# \{ \text{$G$-gradings of $Q \backslash \{x\}$} \}. 
	\]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Given a $G$-grading on $Q \backslash \{x\}$, 
we can assign any element of $G$ to $x$ and obtain a $G$-grading on $Q$,
since $x$ is disconnected from the rest of the quiver.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
There is a generalization of these two results to $G$-balanced exchange matrices. 
	The analogue of an isolated vertex is an index $h$ such that 
	$b_{hi}=0$ for all $1\leq i \leq r$.
	The analogue of a frozen leaf is a frozen index $f$ such that $b_{fi} = 0$ for all $1 \leq i \leq r$ except for exactly one $1 \leq j \leq r$ for which $b_{fj} = \pm 1$. 
	After removing $f$ and freezing $j$, a $G$-grading of the simplified exchange matrix can be extended to a $G$-grading of the original exchange matrix by the formula 
	\[
		\sigma_f = - \frac{1}{b_{fj}} \sum_{i \neq f} b_{ij} \sigma_i. 
	\]
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
We say that a matrix $M$ is \emph{totally positive} if all
of its minors are positive; in other words, every square submatrix
of $M$ has positive determinant.
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
Let $\Sigma = \Sigma^{(n)}$ be the initial seed
shown in 
\cref{fig:initialquiver}, see also \cite[Figure 6.5]{FWZ6}.
(The figure shows the case where $n=4$ but the 
general pattern should be clear.)  
The quiver has $n^2$ total vertices, of which $2n-1$ are frozen.
The initial cluster variables are 
solid minors
which ``stick'' to the left edge 
or the upper edge of the matrix.
Let $\mathcal{A} = \mathcal{A}(\Sigma)$ denote the cluster algebra associated to $\Sigma$.
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:matrices}
There are exactly $2^{2n-1}$ signed cells of the set of 
$n \times n$ matrices, each of which is homeomorphic to an open ball.
	Each signed cell can be obtained from the totally
positive matrices by choosing an arbitrary set of rows, and an arbitrary set of columns, and rescaling these rows and these columns by $-1$.
In other words, if $V^{\sigma}$ is a signed cell
of the space of $n\times n$ matrices, and 
$M=(m_{ij})\in V^{\sigma}$, then its signs are completely
determined by the signs of the entries
$m_{11}, m_{12},\dots, m_{1n}$ and $m_{21}, m_{31}, \dots, m_{n1}$.
	In particular, for $I, J \subset [n]$, with $|I|=|J|=\ell$, we have
	\[
		\operatorname{sign}(M_{I,J}) = \operatorname{sign}(m_{11})^{\ell} \prod_{i\in I} \operatorname{sign}(m_{i1}) \prod_{j\in J} \operatorname{sign}(m_{1j}).
	\]
The analogous result holds for 
arbitrary $G$-gradings: there are exactly $|G|^{2n-1}$ $G$-gradings,
and all of these come from the torus action.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let us use the seed shown in 
\cref{fig:initialquiver}.  Suppose 
we fix the signs of the cluster variables
$z_{i,1}$ and $z_{1,j}$, that is, the signs of the entries 
in the first row and first column of matrix $z$.
This fixes the signs of the cluster variables in the bottom
row of the quiver in \cref{fig:initialquiver}.
Note that $z_{1,1}$ is incident to only one arrow with a vertex
in row $2$.  Thus \eqref{eq:grading2} uniquely determines the 
sign of $z_{12,12}.$  Once we know this sign, \eqref{eq:grading2}
uniquely determines the signs of $z_{23,12}$ and $z_{12,23}$.
We can then propagate this argument and determine the signs
of all cluster variables in the second row of \cref{fig:initialquiver}.
Now we see that $z_{12,12}$ is incident to only one arrow
with a vertex in row $3$.  Thus we can use \eqref{eq:grading2}
to determine the sign of $z_{123,123}$ and all other
cluster variables in the third row.
Continuing in this fashion, we see that if we fix
arbitrary signs for the cluster variables in the bottom row
of \cref{fig:initialquiver}, then  we can find a unique way 
to determine signs for the remaining cluster variables, such that the 
result is a signed seed.  The same argument works for $G$-gradings.

The fact that each signed cell is homeomorphic to an open 
ball is a consequence of \cref{thm:test}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
A matrix is called \emph{sign regular} if for each $k$, 
	all its $k\times k$ minors have
	the same sign or are zero.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
It is well known that totally positive matrices have all positive
eigenvalues.  Moreover, sign regular matrices have all real eigenvalues~\cite{Ando1987}.  
However, square matrices coming from more general signed seeds need not have real eigenvalues.
For example, the matrix 
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
	7 & -7 & 1\\
	4 & -5 & 2\\
	5 & -8 &6 
\end{bmatrix}
\] comes from a signed seed but does not have real eigenvalues.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
A matrix $A$ is \textit{sign symmetric} if $\det A_{\alpha, \beta} \det A_{\beta, \alpha}\geq 0$ for all $\alpha, \beta$. We say a $G$-grading $\sigma : \mathcal{X} \to G$ is \textit{$G$-symmetric} if $\sigma(z_{\alpha, \beta}) = \sigma (z_{\beta, \alpha})$ for all $\alpha, \beta$.
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
A \textbf{valued quiver} is a quiver $Q = (Q_0, Q_1, s, t)$ with the data of an ordered pair of positive integers $(v_1(\alpha), v_2(\alpha)) \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}^2$ to every edge $\alpha \in Q_1$ and a decomposition $Q_0 = Q_0^{\text{mut}} \sqcup Q_0^{\text{fro}}$ of the vertices into mutable and frozen vertices which satisfies the following conditions:
    \begin{enumerate}[label = (\arabic*)]
        \item There are no loops;
        \item There is at most one edge between any pair of vertices, and there are no edges between any pair of frozen vertices;
        \item There is a choice of positive integers $d_i > 0$ for all $i \in Q_0$ such that for any edge $\alpha \in Q_1$ we have $d_{s(\alpha)} v_1 = d_{t(\alpha)} v_2$. 
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
The notion of a valued quiver is equivalent to a symmetrizable exchange matrix. Given a valued quiver, we can define a symmetrizable exchange matrix where 
    \[
        b_{ij} = \begin{cases}
            0 & \text{if there is no edge between $i$ and $j$} \\
            v_1 & \text{if there is an edge $i \xrightarrow{(v_1,v_2)} j$} \\
            -v_2 & \text{if there is an edge $j \xrightarrow{(v_1, v_2)} i$}. 
        \end{cases}
    \]
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
Let $M$ be a $k \times k$ matrix. Let $M_{I}^J$ denote the matrix with the rows indexed by $I$ removed and the columns indexed by $J$ removed. Then, we have the identity
	\[
		\det (M) \det (M^{1, k}_{1, k}) = \det(M^{1}_1) \det (M^k_{k}) - \det(M^k_1) \det (M^1_k). 
	\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:principal-minors}
	For $k \geq 2$, we have 
	\[
		\mathbf{P}_{[k-1]} \mathbf{P}_{[2, k+1]} - \mathbf{P}_{[k+1]} \mathbf{P}_{[2, k-1]} = \frac{\mathbf{P}_{[k+1]} z_{[2, k],[k-1]} z_{[k-1], [2,k]} + \mathbf{P}_{[k-1]} z_{[2, k+1], [k]} z_{[k], [2, k+1]} }{\mathbf{P}_{[k]}}. 
	\]
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
From the Desnanot-Jacobi identity, we have 
	\[
		\mathbf{P}_{[k+1]} \mathbf{P}_{[2,k]} = \mathbf{P}_{[2, k+1]} \mathbf{P}_{[k]} - z_{[2, k+1], [k]} z_{[k], [2, k+1]}.
	\]
	Thus, we can replace the right term in the numerator of the right hand side by 
	\[
		\mathbf{P}_{[k-1]} (\mathbf{P}_{[2, k+1]} \mathbf{P}_{[k]} - \mathbf{P}_{[k+1]} \mathbf{P}_{[2, k]})
	\]
	The numerator is then equal to 
	\[
		\mathbf{P}_{[k]} \mathbf{P}_{[k-1]} \mathbf{P}_{[2, k+1]} - \mathbf{P}_{[k+1]} (\mathbf{P}_{[k-1]} \mathbf{P}_{[2, k]} - z_{[2, k], [k-1]} z_{[k-1], [2,k]}).
	\]
	We can apply the Desnanot-Jacobi identity again to get 
	\[
		\mathbf{P}_{[k]} \mathbf{P}_{[2, k-1]} = \mathbf{P}_{[k-1]} \mathbf{P}_{[2,k]} - z_{[2, k],[k-1]} z_{[k-1], [2,k]}. 
	\]
	This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
Let $2 \leq a < b$ be positive integers. Let $P_I = z_{[|I|], I}$ denote the flag minor corresponding to $I$. Then we have
	\[
		\frac{P_{[a-1, b-1]} P_{[a, b+1]} P_{[a+1, b]} + P_{[a-1, b]} P_{[a, b-1]} P_{[a+1, b+1]}}{P_{[a, b]}} = 
		P_{[a-1, b-1] \cup \{b+1\}} P_{[a+1, b]}
		- 
		P_{[a-1, b]} P_{[a+1, b-1] \cup \{b+1\}}. 
	\]
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
This follows from two applications of the three-term incidence-Pl\"ucker relations for flag minors. We use the following two relations:
	\begin{align}
		P_{[a-1, b-1]} P_{[a, b+1]} & = P_{[a-1, b-1] \cup \{b+1\}} P_{[a, b]} - P_{[a-1, b]} P_{[a, b-1] \cup \{b+1\}} \label{eqn:rel1}\\ 
		P_{[a, b]} P_{[a+1, b-1] \cup \{b+1\}} & =  P_{[a+1, b]} P_{[a, b-1] \cup \{b+1\}} - P_{[a, b-1]} P_{[a+1, b+1]} .\label{eqn:rel2}
	\end{align}
	We have: 
	\begin{align*}
		\mathsf{LHS} & = \frac{(P_{[a-1, b-1]} P_{[a, b+1]}) P_{[a+1, b]} + P_{[a-1, b]} P_{[a, b-1]} P_{[a+1, b+1]}}{P_{[a, b]}} \\
		& = \frac{(P_{[a-1, b-1] \cup \{b+1\}} P_{[a, b]} - P_{[a-1, b]} P_{[a, b-1] \cup \{b+1\}})P_{[a+1, b]} + P_{[a-1, b]} P_{[a, b-1]} P_{[a+1, b+1]}}{P_{[a,b]}}\\
		& = P_{[a-1, b-1] \cup \{b+1\}} P_{[a+1, b]} + \frac{P_{[a-1, b]}}{P_{[a, b]}} \left ( P_{[a, b-1]} P_{[a+1, b+1]} - P_{[a+1, b]} P_{[a, b-1] \cup \{b+1\}} \right ) \\
		& = P_{[a-1, b-1] \cup \{b+1\}} P_{[a+1, b]} + \frac{P_{[a-1, b]}}{P_{[a, b]}} \cdot (- P_{[a, b]} P_{[a+1, b-1] \cup \{b+1\}}) \\
		& = P_{[a-1, b-1] \cup \{b+1\}} P_{[a+1, b]} - P_{[a-1, b]} P_{[a+1, b-1] \cup \{b+1\}} = \mathsf{RHS}.
	\end{align*}
	where the second equality follows from~\cref{eqn:rel1} and the fourth equality follows from~\cref{eqn:rel2}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:symmetric-minors-irred-coprime}
	For any subsets $I, J \subseteq [n]$ of the same size, let $z_{I, J}$ denote the matrix minor in $\mathcal{A}_{\text{sym}}$ corresponding to row set $I$ and column set $J$. Then, the collection of matrix minors $\{z_{I, J}\}$ are irreducible.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
We induct on the size $|I| = |J| = k$. For the base case $k = 1$, the matrix minors are matrix entries, which are clearly irreducible. Now, we prove that $z_{I, J}$ if irreducible under the assumption that smaller minors are irreducible and $k \geq 2$. 
	
	We first consider the case $I \neq J$. Pick some $i \in I \backslash J$, then via Laplace expansion we can write 
	\[
		z_{I, J} = \sum_{j \in J} \Delta_j \cdot z_{i, j}, \quad \quad \quad  \Delta_j = \pm z_{I \backslash \{i\}, J \backslash \{j\}}.
	\] 
	Consider an arbitrary factorization $z_{I, J} = P(\mathbf{z}) Q(\mathbf{z})$. When we view both sides as polynomials in $z_{i, j}$ with $j \in J$ over the UFD $R_i := \mathbb{C}[\{z_{a,b} : a \in I \backslash \{i\}, b \in J\}]$, we get an equality of the form 
	\[
		\sum_{j \in J} \Delta_j \cdot z_{i, j} = \left (C + \sum_{j \in J} A_j z_{i, j} \right ) \left ( D + \sum_{j \in J} B_j z_{i, j} \right ), \quad A_j, B_j, C, D \in R_i[z_{i, j}, j \in J].
	\]
	We cannot have that $A_j \neq 0$ for some $j$ and $B_{j'} \neq 0$ for some $j'$ because then the right hand side would be degree $2$ over $z_{i, j}$, $j \in J$. Thus, we can assume without loss of generality that $A_j = 0$ for all $j \in J$. This implies that $D = 0$, and all $\Delta_j$ have a common factor $C$. But from the inductive hypothesis, the $\Delta_j$ are distinct and irreducible. Hence, $C$ must be a unit. This proves that $z_{I, J}$ is irreducible. 

	We now show that determinants of generic symmetric matrices
	are irreducible.\footnote{We expect that this result is well-known
	but couldn't find a published reference.}
	Now consider the case where $I = J$, i.e. $z_{I, J}$ is a principal minor. It suffices to prove that if $M_n = [z_{i,j}]_{1 \leq i, j \leq n}$ is a generic symmetric matrix with $z_{i,j} = z_{j,i}$, then $\det (M_n)$ is an irreducible polynomial. Consider an arbitrary factorization 
	\[
		\det (M_n) = P(\mathbf{z}) Q(\mathbf{z}). 
	\] 
	Consider $P$ and $Q$ as polynomials in $z_{n, n}$. Since $\det(M_n)$ is linear in $z_{n, n}$, we can assume without loss of generality that $P(z)$ is linear in $z_{n, n}$ and $Q(z)$ is independent of $z_{n,n}$. For any $1 \leq k < n$, $Q(z)$ must be independent of $z_{k, n}$ or else $\det(M_n)$ would contain terms like $z_{n, n} z_{k, n}$. Hence $P(z)$ contains terms with $z_{k, n}$ for all $1 \leq k < n$. By similarly reasoning, $Q(z)$ must be independent of $z_{k, k}$. Hence $P(z)$ contains terms with $z_{k, k}$ for all $1 \leq k < n$. Finally, we can repeat the same argument to conclude that $Q(z)$ is independent of all variables $z_{a, b}$, i.e. it is constant. This suffices for the proof.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
The cluster algebra given by the initial seed in \cref{eqn:symmetric-initial-n=5-with-variables} is a cluster structure for $\mathcal{A}_{\text{sym}}$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
We first prove $\mathcal{U}(Q) \subseteq \mathcal{A}_{\text{sym}}$ using~\cite[Proposition 6.4.1]{FWZ6}. It is enough to show that whenever $x$ is an initial cluster variable, then $x' \in \mathcal{A}_{\text{sym}}$ and $x'$ is coprime to $x$ and that all initial cluster variables are pairwise coprime. The fact that the initial variables are pairwise coprime already follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:symmetric-minors-irred-coprime}. Note that the one-step exchange relations in~\cref{eqn:symmetric-initial-n=5-with-variables} are exactly the same as the one-step exchange relations as~\cref{fig:initialquiver}. Thus, to compute $x'$ for an initial cluster variable $x \in \mathcal{X}_{\text{sym}}$, we can compute the mutation in the initial quiver for $\text{Mat}_{n \times n}$ and then identify $z_{ij} = z_{ji}$ for all $i, j$. 
	
	For any cluster variable $x = z_{1, k}$ on the first row, we get that $x' = z_{1, k-1} z_{2, k+1} - z_{1, k+1} z_{2,k}$ for $k \geq 2$ which is clearly coprime from $z_{1, k}$ and $x' = z_{1,2}$ for $k = 1$ which is coprime to $z_{1, 1}$. For any cluster variable $x = \mathbf{P}_{[k]}$ on the left-most boundary, Lemma~\ref{lem:principal-minors} implies that $x' = \mathbf{P}_{[k-1]} \mathbf{P}_{[2, k+1]} - \mathbf{P}_{[k+1]} \mathbf{P}_{[2, k-1]}$. Suppose for the sake of contradiction that $x$ and $x'$ were not coprime. Since $\mathbf{P}_{[k]}$ is irreducible in $\mathcal{A}_{\text{sym}}$, we must have for some $f \in \mathcal{A}_{\text{sym}}$ and $g \in \mathcal{A}_{\text{sym}}$ independent of $z_{k+1, k+1}$:
	\begin{align*}
		\mathbf{P}_{[k]} \cdot f & = \mathbf{P}_{[k-1]} \mathbf{P}_{[2, k+1]} - \mathbf{P}_{[k+1]} \mathbf{P}_{[2, k-1]} \\
		& = (\mathbf{P}_{[k-1]} \mathbf{P}_{[2, k]} - \mathbf{P}_{[k]} \mathbf{P}_{[2, k-1]}) z_{k+1, k+1} + g. 
	\end{align*}
	Since the right hand side is linear in $z_{k+1, k+1}$, $f$ must also be linear in $z_{k+1, k+1}$ and we must have 
	\[
		\mathbf{P}_{[k]} \,  | \,  \mathbf{P}_{[k-1]} \mathbf{P}_{[2, k]} - \mathbf{P}_{[k]} \mathbf{P}_{[2, k-1]} \implies \mathbf{P}_{[k]} \, | \, \mathbf{P}_{[k-1]} \mathbf{P}_{[2, k]}. 
	\]
	But this is a contradiction. Finally, any other cluster variable $x = P_{[a, b]}$ for positive integer $2 \leq a < b$ has 
	\[
		x' = P_{[a-1, b]} P_{[a+1, b-1] \cup \{b+1\}} - P_{[a-1, b-1] \cup \{b+1\}} P_{[a+1, b]}.
	\]
	When we let $z_{i, b} = 0$ for $1 \leq i \leq b-a + 1$, we get $x = 0$ and $x' = z_{b-a+2, b} P_{[a-1, b-1] \cup \{b+1\}}$. This implies that $x \nmid x'$ and proves that $x$ and $x'$ are coprime. 


	To prove $\mathcal{A}_{\text{sym}} \subseteq \mathcal{A}(Q)$, we want to find a mutation sequence which lets us get the generators $z_{ij}$ for $1 \leq i \leq j \leq n$ as cluster variables. We provide this mutation sequence by inducting on the $n$. The inductive hypothesis is for all smaller $n$ we can find a mutation sequence where all of the matrix entries are realized as cluster variables. 
	
	When we mutate the bottom row from left to right, the row above from left to right, and so on, then we get the quiver in  the first row from left to right, the second row from left to right, the third row from left to right, and so on, we get the quiver in~\cref{eqn:mutated-quiver-symmetric}. Note that the bottom part of the valued quiver is the initial valued quiver for $n-1$ but all of the indices are translated up by $1$. From the inductive hypothesis, we can get $z_{i, j}$ for $2 \leq i \leq j \leq n$ and the entries $z_{1,1}, \ldots, z_{1, n}$ are already in the initial quiver. This suffices for the proof. 

An alternative way to check that $\mathcal{A}_{\text{sym}} \subseteq \mathcal{A}(Q)$ is to use a centrally symmetric version of double wiring diagrams, and show that 
	each entry $z_{i,j}$ lies in such a centrally symmetric double wiring diagram. For the non-centrally symmetric case, see~\cite[Section 6.6]{FWZ6}. The argument for the centrally symmetric case is similar. 
	\begin{equation} \label{eqn:mutated-quiver-symmetric}\begin{tikzcd}
    {\boxed{12345,12345}} &&&&& \\
    {2345,2345} && {\boxed{1234,2345}} \\
    {234,234} && {234,345} & {\boxed{123,345}} \\
    {23,23} && {23,34} & {23,45} & {\boxed{12,45}} \\
    {2,2} && {2,3} & {2,4} & {2,5} & {\boxed{1,5}}
    \arrow[from=1-1, to=2-1]
    \arrow[from=2-1, to=3-1]
    \arrow["{(2,1)}"{description}, from=2-3, to=2-1]
    \arrow[from=2-3, to=3-3]
    \arrow["{(1,2)}"{description}, from=3-1, to=3-3]
    \arrow[from=3-1, to=4-1]
    \arrow[from=3-3, to=3-4]
    \arrow[from=3-3, to=4-3]
    \arrow[from=3-4, to=4-4]
    \arrow["{(1,2)}"{description}, from=4-1, to=4-3]
    \arrow[from=4-1, to=5-1]
    \arrow["{(2,1)}"{description}, from=4-3, to=3-1]
    \arrow[from=4-3, to=4-4]
    \arrow[from=4-3, to=5-3]
    \arrow[from=4-4, to=4-5]
    \arrow[from=4-4, to=5-4]
    \arrow[from=4-5, to=5-5]
    \arrow["{(1,2)}"{description}, from=5-1, to=5-3]
    \arrow["{(2,1)}"{description}, from=5-3, to=4-1]
    \arrow[from=5-3, to=5-4]
    \arrow[from=5-4, to=4-3]
    \arrow[from=5-4, to=5-5]
    \arrow[from=5-5, to=5-6]
\end{tikzcd}\end{equation}
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
There are $|G|^{n}$ $G$-gradings for the cluster algebra $\mathcal{A}_{\text{sym}}$. The different $G$-gradings are determined by the $G$-degrees of $z_{1, 1}$ and $z_{[k], [2, k+1]}$ for $1 \leq k \leq n-1$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Consider the columns $3, 4, \ldots, n$ in the initial quiver and repeatedly apply Lemma~\ref{lem:frozen-leaf} by ``shedding'' the outside frozen vertices until we have removed all vertices in these columns. We are left with the following quiver (which we have drawn for the $n = 5$ case): 
	\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{\boxed{X_{15}}} && \\
		{X_{10}} && {\boxed{X_{14}}} \\
	\\
	{X_6} && {\boxed{X_9}} \\
	\\
	{X_3} && {\boxed{X_5}} \\
	\\
	{X_1} && {\boxed{X_2}}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["{(1,2)}", from=2-1, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=4-1]
	\arrow["{(1,2)}"{description}, from=4-1, to=4-3]
	\arrow[from=4-1, to=6-1]
	\arrow["{(2,1)}"{description}, from=4-3, to=2-1]
	\arrow["{(1,2)}"{description}, from=6-1, to=6-3]
	\arrow[from=6-1, to=8-1]
	\arrow["{(2,1)}"{description}, from=6-3, to=4-1]
	\arrow["{(1,2)}", from=8-1, to=8-3]
	\arrow["{(2,1)}"{description}, from=8-3, to=6-1]
\end{tikzcd}\]
	Then repeatedly apply Lemma~\ref{lem:frozen-leaf} to the first column from top to bottom.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
In the paper~\cite{ross2023duallylorentzianpolynomials}, the authors give a lemma about non-negative symmetric matrices which allows one to check the Lorentzian property. Consider a symmetric $m \times m$ matrix $M$ with non-negative entries. Then, they show that $M$ has at most one positive eigenvalue if and only if for every $I \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, m\}$, we have $(-1)^{|I|} \det M_I \leq 0$ where $M_I$ denotes the principal minor of $M$ associated to $I$. It is an interesting question to ask if the signs $(-1)^{|I|} \det M_I \leq 0$ are compatible with one of the $2^{n}$ signed cells on $\mathcal{A}_{\text{sym}}$ that we have just constructed. Unfortunately, it is easy to see that none of the signed cells we've constructed can have the signs $(-1)^{|I|} \det M_I \leq 0$. Indeed, looking at the cluster variable $z_{1, 1}$, we immediately see that $z_{12, 12} \geq 0$. In particular, this provides an example where the signed cells do not cover the whole cluster variety. More generally, since the signs of the leading principal minors in a given signed seed of $\mathcal{A}_{\text{sym}}$ are predetermined, the eigenvalue signature is determined from Sylvester's law of inertia.\footnote{Recall that one version of Sylvester's law of inertia states that when every principal minor is non-zero, then the number of negative eigenvalues is equal to the number of sign changes in the sequence $\mathbf{P}_{\emptyset} := 1, \mathbf{P}_{[1]}, \mathbf{P}_{[2]}, \ldots, \mathbf{P}_{[n]}.$}
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
Is there another cluster structure on symmetric matrices where the sign pattern $(-1)^{|I|} \det M_I < 0$ gives a signed cell?
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- definition-20: body_md -->
Let $R = (r_1, \ldots, r_m)$ and $S = (s_1, \ldots, s_m)$ be two sequences of elements in $[n]$. Then, we define $z_{R, S}$ to be the determinant of the $R \times S$ submatrix of $(z_{i,j})_{1 \leq i, j \leq n}$. Explicitly, we have 
	\[
		z_{R, S} := \sum_{\sigma \in \mathfrak{S}_m} \operatorname{sign}(\sigma) \prod_{i = 1}^m z_{r_i s_{\sigma(i)}} \in \operatorname{Sk}_n. 
	\]
	For a sequence $I = (i_1 , \ldots , i_d)$ of elements in $[n]$, we define $P_I$ denote the \textbf{flag minor} $z_{[d], I}$. If $I_1, \ldots, I_k$ are sequences of elements in $[n]$, we also write $P_{I_1 \ldots I_k}$ for the flag minor corresponding to the concatenation of $I_1, \ldots, I_k$. If $S \subseteq [n]$, we write $P_S$ for the flag minor corresponding to the sequence consisting of elements of $S$ written in increasing order.
<!-- end definition-20 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:3-term-plucker}
	For $\ell \geq 0$, let $S \in [n]^{\ell}$ be any sequence of length $\ell$. 
	Let $i, j, k \in [n] \backslash S$ be distinct indices. Then, we have 
	\[
		P_{ijS}P_{k S} - P_{ikS} P_{jS} + P_{jk S} P_{iS} = 0. 
	\]
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- definition-21: body_md -->
Let $I = (i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_d) \in [n]^d$. We define the \textbf{Pfaffian}, denoted  $\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_I$, inductively via the following rules: 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item If $d$ is odd, then $\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_I = 0$.
        \item $\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{\emptyset} = 1$
        \item If $d = 2$, then $\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{(i_1, i_2)} = z_{i_1,i_2}$. 
		\item
		    For $d \geq 3$, we define $\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_I = \sum_{r = 2}^d (-1)^r z_{i_1,i_r} \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{i_2, \ldots, \widehat{i_r}, \ldots, i_{d}} $
    \end{enumerate}
	For a subset $S \subset [n]$, we denote by $\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_S$ the Pfaffian corresponding to the elements of $S$ sorted in increasing order.
<!-- end definition-21 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:brill-theorem}
    Let $R, S \in {[n]}^m$. Then, the following identity holds in $\operatorname{Sk}_n$:
    \[
        z_{R, S} = {(-1)}^{\lfloor \frac{m}{2} \rfloor} \sum_{k = 0}^{\lfloor \frac{m}{2} \rfloor} {(-1)}^k \sum_{\substack{|w| = 2k \\ w \subseteq R}} \operatorname{sign} \binom{R}{w(R \backslash w)} \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_w \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{(R\backslash w)S}.
    \]
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:brill-theorem-extremal-case}
	\phantom{h}
	\begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*)]
		\item When $S = \{1, \ldots, \widehat{i}, \ldots, 2d, j\}$ for $1 \leq i \leq 2d$ and $j > 2d$, we have 
		\[
			P_S = \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[1, 2d]} \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_S. 
		\]
		\item When $S = \{1, \ldots, \widehat{i}, \ldots, 2d+1, j\}$ for $1 \leq i \leq 2d+1$ and $j > 2d+1$, we have 
		\[
			P_S = \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[1, 2d+1] \backslash \{i\}} \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[1, 2d+1] \cup \{j\}}. 
		\]
		\item When $S = \{1, \ldots, \widehat{i}, \ldots, \widehat{j}, \ldots, 2d, k, \ell\}$ for $1 \leq i < j \leq 2d$ and $2d < k < \ell$, we have 
		\[
			P_S = \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[1, 2d]} \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_S  - \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[1, 2d] \backslash \{i, j\}} \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[1, 2d] \cup \{k, \ell\}}.  
		\]
		\item When $S = \{1, \ldots, \widehat{i}, \ldots, \widehat{j}, \ldots, 2d+1, k, \ell\}$ for $1 \leq i < j \leq 2d+1$ and $2d+1 < k < \ell$, we have 
		\[
			P_S = \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[1, 2d+1] \backslash \{i\}} \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[1, 2d+1] \backslash \{j\}, k, \ell} - \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[1, 2d+1] \backslash \{j\}} \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[1, 2d+1] \backslash \{i\}, k, \ell}. 
		\]
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
There are $|G|^n$ distinct $G$-gradings on the cluster algebra structure of $\operatorname{Sk}_n$ for $n \geq 3$. Moreover, the $G$-gradings are determined by the $G$-degrees of the variables $\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{1,2}, \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{1,3}, \ldots, \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{1,n}$, and $\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{2,3}$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:frozen-leaf} repeatedly on the last column of \cref{figure:initial-seed-for-skew-symmetric-matrices-n=7} from bottom to top. We are left with the initial quiver for $\operatorname{Sk}_{n-1}$ and an isolated vertex. From Lemma~\ref{lem:isolated-vertex}, we have
	\[
		\# \{\text{$G$-gradings on $\operatorname{Sk}_n$}\} = |G| \cdot \# \{\text{$G$-gradings on $\operatorname{Sk}_{n-1}$}\}. 
	\]
	We get that the number of $G$-gradings on $\operatorname{Sk}_n$ is $|G|^n$ by induction.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group. Then there are $|G|^n / |G[2]|$ gradings which come from the torus action. As a consequence, there are $|G[2]|$ distinct gradings up to the torus action.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
For $2 \leq k \leq n$, the torus degree is given by $\deg (\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{1, k}) = \mathbf{e}_1 + \mathbf{e}_k$. Let $\mathbf{g} = (g_1, \ldots, g_n) \in G^{\oplus n}$ be an element in the kernel of $\Psi_G : G^{\oplus n} \to \mathfrak{gr}(\operatorname{Sk}_n, G)$. Then, $g_1 + g_k = 0$ for all $2 \leq k \leq n$ and $\mathbf{g}$ is in the form 
	\[
		\mathbf{g} = (g, -g, -g, \ldots, -g)
	\]
	for some $g \in G$. From $\deg (\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{2, 3})$, we necessarily need $2g = 0$. Finally, the condition $2g = 0$ is enough to guarantee that $\mathbf{g}$ is in the kernel since all degrees of initial cluster variables lie in the subgroup 
	\[
		\{(t_1, \ldots, t_n) \in \mathbb{Z}^n : t_1 + \cdots + t_n \equiv 0 \pmod 2 \}. 
	\]
	Thus, $\ker \Psi_G \cong G[2]$ which suffices for the proof.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\cite[Theorem 1.4]{skew}\footnote{Our
	minors are the transpose of the minors listed in~\cite[Theorem 1.4]{skew}. We have changed the signs accordingly to match the current convention.} 
	\label{thm:total-positivity-test-skew}
	A skew-symmetric matrix $A$ is totally positive if and only if
	\[
		\operatorname{sign} \left ( P_{[1, j-1] \cup [n-k+j, n]} \right ) = (-1)^{k + (n-j)(n-k)} \text{ for any } 1 \leq j \leq k \leq n-1. 
	\]
	When this holds, we also have $\operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_I) = (-1)^{\sum_{i \in I} i - \binom{|I| + 1}{2}}$ for all subsets $I \subseteq [n]$ of even size. As one special case, we have 
	\[
		\operatorname{sign} (  P_{[1,a] \cup [b, n]} ) = (-1)^{ab + n(a + b)} \text{ for } a < b \text{ and } b-a \geq 2. 
	\]
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:irreducible-factors-of-skew}
    When $n = 2m$ is even, the distinct irreducible factors of the minors in Theorem~\ref{thm:total-positivity-test-skew} are
    \begin{equation}
		\begin{cases}
			\mathcal{M}_1 & = \{ P_{[j-1] \cup [n-k+j, n]}  \mid 1 \leq j < k \leq n-2 \} \\ 
			\mathcal{M}_2 & = \{ \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k]}\mid 1 \leq k \leq m \} \\
			\mathcal{M}_3 & = \{\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-1] \cup\{n\}}  \mid 1 \leq k \leq m-1 \} \\
			\mathcal{M}_4 & = \{\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-1] \backslash \{k\}}\mid 1 \leq k \leq n-2 \}.
		\end{cases}
	\end{equation}
    When $n = 2m-1$ is odd, the distinct irreducible factors of the minors in Theorem~\ref{thm:total-positivity-test-skew} are 
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{cases}
			\mathcal{M}_1 & = \{ P_{[j-1] \cup [n-k+j, n]} \mid 1 \leq j < k \leq n-2 \} \\
			\mathcal{M}_2 & = \{ \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k]} \mid 1 \leq k \leq m-1 \} \\
			\mathcal{M}_3 & = \{ \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-1] \cup \{n\}} \mid 1 \leq k \leq m-1 \} \\
			\mathcal{M}_4 & = \{ \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n] \backslash \{k\}} \mid 1 \leq k \leq n-2 \}. 
		\end{cases}
	\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
Let $M = (x_{ij})$ be a skew-symmetric matrix with indeterminate entries. Then $z_{I, J}$ is irreducible if and only if $|I \Delta J| \geq 4$, where $I \Delta J$ denotes the symmetric difference of $I$ and $J$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
From Corollary~\ref{cor:brill-theorem-extremal-case}, $z_{I, J}$ is reducible when $|I \Delta J| \leq 2$. It remains to prove that $z_{I, J}$ is irreducible when $|I \Delta J| \geq 4$. Equivalently, consider a $n \times n$ matrix $(X_{ij})_{1 \leq i, j \leq n}$ and let $1 \leq k \leq n-2$. We want to prove that the determinant polynomial remains irreducible when we set $X_{ji} = -X_{ij}$ for all $1 \leq i < j \leq k$ and $X_{ii} = 0$ for $1 \leq i \leq k$. It is enough to prove this for the case $k = n-2$. Indeed, if the determinant polynomial becomes factorizable for $k < n-2$, then it must be a homogeneous factorization. To recover the determinant polynomial for $k = n-2$, we specialize some of the diagonal variables to $0$ and $X_{ij} = -X_{ji}$ for some more indices $i, j$, we preserve the homogeneous degrees of the factors. Hence, we either get that the determinant polynomial for $k = n-2$ is zero or is factorizable. For the rest of the proof, we prove that the determinant is irreducible in the $k = n-2$ case, i.e. the case where $|I \Delta J| = 4$. 
    
    In this case, we have $I = S \cup \{a, b\}$ and $J = S \cup \{c, d\}$ where $a, b, c, d$ are distinct indices. When $S = \emptyset$, then $z_{I, J}$ is the determinant of a generic $2 \times 2$ matrix, which is irreducible. 
	
	Now let $|S| > 0$ and without loss of generality, we can assume $\max(S) < a < b$ and $\max (S) < c < d$. The polynomial $z_{I, J}$ is linear in each of the collection of variables $\{X_{a, *}\}$, $\{ X_{b, *} \} $, $\{ X_{*, c} \}$, and $\{ X_{*, d} \}$. For example, using Laplace expansion in the $a$th row and Corollary~\ref{cor:brill-theorem-extremal-case}, we get the formula 
	\begin{equation}\label{eqn:laplace-expansion-of-skew-determinant}
		z_{I, J} = \sum_{s \in S} X_{as} \cdot Y_s
	\end{equation}
	where the $Y_s$ are products of two Pfaffians not containing any variable of the form $X_{a*}$. We can find similar formulas for $X_{b,*}$, $X_{*, c}$, and $X_{*, d}$. In particular, this implies that $z_{I, J}$ is non-zero and any variables of the form $X_{a, *}$, $X_{b, *}$, $X_{*, c}$, and $X_{*, d}$ appears in $z_{I, J}$ with non-zero coefficient. 
	
	Suppose for the sake of contradiction that $z_{I, J} = P \cdot Q$ for $P, Q$ non-trivial. Without loss of generality, we can assume that $X_{a, c}$ appears in $P$ and not $Q$. Since $z_{I, J}$ is linear in the collections $\{X_{a, *}\}$ and $\{X_{*, c}\}$, this implies that any variable of the form $X_{a, *}$ and $X_{*, c}$ appears in $P$ and does not appear in $Q$ since $X_{a, c} X_{a, *}$ or $X_{a, c} X_{*, c}$ is forbidden to appear in the product. Thus, $X_{a, d}$ and $X_{b, c}$ appear in $P$, and by the same argument all variables of the form $X_{a, *}, X_{b, *}, X_{*, c}$, and $X_{*, d}$ appear in $P$ and $Q \in \mathbb{C}[X_{s_1s_2}]_{s_1,s_2 \in S}$. From Equation~\ref{eqn:laplace-expansion-of-skew-determinant}, it is clear that $Q$ must be trivial since Pfaffians are irreducible. This suffices for the proof.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:proof-of-positivity-test-matches-cluster-structure}
Recall the extended cluster 
	$\{x_{(r,c)}\}$ from 
    \eqref{eqn:initial-cluster-skew-symmetric-matrices}.
	Then the assignment $\operatorname{sign}(x_{(r, c)}) = (-1)^{rc}$ defines a signed seed 
	$\sigma_{Sk}$ on $\operatorname{Sk}_n$. Using $\sigma_{Sk}$, the irreducible factors in Proposition~\ref{prop:irreducible-factors-of-skew} get the signs specified in Theorem~\ref{thm:total-positivity-test-skew}. As a consequence, a skew-symmetric matrix is totally positive 
if and only if it comes from the signed seed $\sigma_{Sk}$ of the cluster algebra on $\operatorname{Sk}_n$.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\cite[Theorem 6]{Speyer} shows that there are many skew-symmetric matrices all of whose
Pfaffians are nonnegative.  This subset of skew-symmetric matrices is different
from the totally positive subset of skew-symmetric matrices from 
\cref{thm:proof-of-positivity-test-matches-cluster-structure}; it would be interesting
to explore whether there is a relation.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Fix some point of the cluster torus defined by the initial seed from which we can evaluate our cluster variables. We will prove the following two claims by simultaneous induction which are equivalent to the total positivity test from~\cite{skew}. 

	\textbf{Claim 1.} Let $n = 2m$ be even. Suppose that the following expressions are real-valued with
	\[
		\begin{cases}
			\text{$\operatorname{sign} \left (\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{1,k} \right ) = (-1)^k$} \quad & \text{for $3 \leq k \leq n$.} \\
			\text{$\operatorname{sign} \left (\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k]} \right ) = 1$} \quad & \text{for $1 \leq k \leq m$.} \\
			\text{$\operatorname{sign} \left (\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2, 2k-1]} \right ) = 1$} \quad & \text{for $2 \leq k \leq m$.} \\
			\text{$\operatorname{sign}(P_{[i, j]}) = (-1)^{ij}$} \quad & \text{for $3 \leq i < j \leq n$}
		\end{cases}
	\]
	Then, the following expressions are real-valued with 
	\[
		\begin{cases}
			\text{$\operatorname{sign} \left ( \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k]} \right ) = 1$} \quad & \text{for $1 \leq k \leq m$}, \\
			\text{$\operatorname{sign} (P_{[j, n]}) = 1$} \quad & \text{for $3 \leq j \leq n-1$}, \\
			\text{$\operatorname{sign} (P_{[a] \cup [b, n]}) = (-1)^{ab}$} \quad & \text{for $4 \leq a+3 \leq b \leq n-1$}, \\
			\text{$\operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-1] \backslash \{i\}}) = (-1)^{i+1}$} \quad & \text{for $1 \leq i \leq n-2$} \\
			\text{$ \operatorname{sign} \left ( \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-1]  \cup \{n\}} \right ) = 1$} \quad & \text{for $1 \leq k \leq m-1$}. 
		\end{cases}
	\]

	\textbf{Claim 2.} Let $n = 2m+1$ be odd. Suppose that the following expressions are real-valued with  
	\[
		\begin{cases}
			\text{$\operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{1,k}) = (-1)^k$} \quad & \text{for $3 \leq k \leq n$} \\
			\text{$\operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k]}) = 1$} \quad & \text{for $1 \leq k \leq m$} \\
			\text{$\operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2, 2k+1]}) = 1$} \quad & \text{for $1 \leq k \leq m$} \\
			\text{$\operatorname{sign}(P_{[i, j]}) = (-1)^{ij}$} \quad & \text{for $3 \leq i < j \leq n$}
		\end{cases}
	\]
	Then, the following expressions are real-valued with 
	\[
		\begin{cases}
			\text{$\operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k]}) = 1$} \quad & \text{for $1 \leq k \leq m$}, \\ 
			\text{$\operatorname{sign}(P_{[j, n]}) = (-1)^j$} \quad & \text{for $3 \leq j \leq n-1$}, \\
			\text{$\operatorname{sign}(P_{[a] \cup [b, n]}) = (-1)^{ab+a+b}$} \quad & \text{for $4 \leq a+3 \leq b \leq n-1$} \\
			\text{$\operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n] \backslash \{i\}}) = (-1)^{i+1}$} \quad & \text{for $1 \leq i \leq n-2$} \\
			\text{$\operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-1] \cup \{n\}}) = -1$} \quad & \text{for $1 \leq k \leq m-1$} \\
			\text{$\operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-1] \cup \{n\}}) = -1$} \quad & \text{for $k = m$}. 
		\end{cases}
	\] 
	It is easy to check the two claims for $n = 4$ and $n = 5$. Let's prove the claim for $n = 2m$ where $m \geq 3$ assuming that Claim 1 and Claim 2 are true for all smaller values of $n$. Since the inductive hypothesis of $n = 2m$ includes the inductive hypothesis for $n-1 = 2m-1$, we have
	\[
		\begin{cases}
			\text{$\operatorname{sign} (P_{[j, n-1]}) = (-1)^{j}$} \quad & \text{for $3 \leq j \leq n-2$} \\
			\text{$\operatorname{sign}(P_{[a] \cup [b,n-1]}) = (-1)^{ab + a + b}$} \quad & \text{for $4 \leq a +3 \leq b \leq n-2$} \\
			\text{$\operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-1] \backslash \{i\}}) = (-1)^{i+1}$} \quad & \text{for $1 \leq i \leq n-3$} \\
			\text{$\operatorname{sign} (\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-1] \cup \{n-1\}}) = -1$} \quad & \text{for $1 \leq k \leq m-2$} \\ 
			\text{$\operatorname{sign} (\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-1] \cup \{n-1\}}) = -1$} \quad & \text{for $k = m-1$}.     
		\end{cases}
	\]
	In general, for $3 \leq a+3 \leq b \leq n-1$, Proposition~\ref{prop:3-term-plucker} gives the relation
	\begin{equation}\label{eqn:inductive-3-term-plucker}
		P_{[a] \cup [b, n-1]} P_{[a+1] \cup [b+1, n]} = P_{[a+1] \cup [b+1, n-1]} P_{[a] \cup [b, n]} + P_{[a+1] \cup [b, n-1]} P_{[a] \cup [b+1, n]}. 
	\end{equation}
	In the special case where $b -a = 3$, we can further factor the term $P_{[a+1] \cup [b, n-1]}$ using Corollary~\ref{cor:brill-theorem-extremal-case}
	\begin{equation}\label{eqn:factorization-of-minor}
		P_{[a+1] \cup [b, n-1]} =
		\begin{cases}
			\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-2]} \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-1] \backslash \{a+2\}} & \text{ if $n$ is even} \\
			\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-1]}\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-2] \backslash \{a+2\}} & \text{ if $n$ is odd}. 
		\end{cases}
	\end{equation}
	We will use this relation to prove that $\operatorname{sign} (P_{[a] \cup [b, n]}) = (-1)^{ab}$ for all $4 \leq a+3 \leq b \leq n-1$. Consider the possible pairs $(a, b)$ satisfying $4 \leq a + 3 \leq b \leq n-1$ in lexicographic order where $(a, b) < (a', b')$ if and only if $a < a'$ or $a = a'$ and $b < b'$. We prove the claim from lowest to highest in lexicographic order. For the base case $a = 1$ and $b = 4$, we can compute  
	\begin{align*}
		P_{[1] \cup [4, n]} P_{[3, n-1]} & = P_{[1] \cup [4, n-1]} P_{[3, n]} + P_{[1] \cup [3, n-1]} P_{[4, n]} \\ 
		& = P_{[1] \cup [4, n-1]} P_{[3, n]} + \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-1] \backslash \{2\}} \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-2]} P_{[4, n]}. 
	\end{align*}
	From the inductive hypothesis, this implies that $\operatorname{sign}(P_{[1] \cup [4, n]}) = 1$ which matches the claim. In general, from \cref{eqn:inductive-3-term-plucker}, we have 
	\begin{equation}\label{eqn:minor-equation-1}
		P_{[a+1] \cup [b+1, n]} = \begin{dcases*}
			\frac{P_{[a+1] \cup [b+1, n-1]} P_{[a] \cup [b, n]} + P_{[a+1] \cup [b, n-1]} P_{[a] \cup [b+1, n]}}{P_{[a] \cup [b, n-1]}} & \text{if $b-a \geq 4$} \\
			\frac{P_{[a+1] \cup [b+1, n-1]} P_{[a] \cup [b, n]} + \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-2]} \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-1] \backslash \{a+2\}} P_{[a] \cup [b+1, n]}}{P_{[a] \cup [b, n-1]}} & \text{if $b-a = 3$}. 
		\end{dcases*}
	\end{equation}
	The inductive hypothesis gives $\operatorname{sign} ( P_{[1, a+1] \cup [b+1, n]})  = (-1)^{(a+1)(b+1)}$ which verifies that these types of minors have the desired signs. Now, for $n$ even, it remains to show that $\operatorname{sign} (\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-1] \cup \{n\}}) = 1$ for $1 \leq k \leq m-1$. From the inductive hypothesis, this already holds for $k = 1$. For $k \geq 2$, Corollary~\ref{cor:brill-theorem-extremal-case} gives us the relation 
	\begin{equation}
		\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-1] \cup \{n\}} \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-3] \cup \{n-1\}} = P_{[2k-3] \cup \{n-1, n\}} + \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-1] \cup \{n-1\}} \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-3] \cup \{n\}}. 
	\end{equation}
	From the inductive hypothesis, we get $\operatorname{sign} (\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-1] \cup \{n\}}) = 1$ which completes the induction for the case $n$ is even. 

	The proof of the claim for $n = 2m+1$ where $m \geq 3$ is similar. We assume that Claim 1 and Claim 2 are true for all smaller values of $n$. In particular, the claim is true for $n-1 = 2m$ which gives 
\[
\begin{cases}
	\text{$\operatorname{sign} (P_{[j, n-1]}) = 1$} \quad & \text{for $3 \leq j \leq n-2$}, \\
	\text{$\operatorname{sign} (P_{[a] \cup [b, n-1]}) = (-1)^{ab}$} \quad & \text{for $4 \leq a+3 \leq b \leq n-2$}, \\
	\text{$\operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-2] \backslash \{i\}}) = (-1)^{i+1}$} \quad & \text{for $1 \leq i \leq n-3$} \\
	\text{$ \operatorname{sign} \left ( \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-1]  \cup \{n-1\}} \right ) = 1$} \quad & \text{for $1 \leq k \leq m-1$}. 
\end{cases}
\]
To prove that for $4 \leq a + 3 \leq b \leq n-1$ we have $\operatorname{sign} (P_{[a] \cup [b, n]}) = (-1)^{ab + a + b}$, we similarly induct based on the lexicographic order of $(a, b)$. We have 
\[
	P_{[a+1] \cup [b+1, n]} = \begin{dcases*}
		\frac{P_{[a+1] \cup [b+1, n-1]} P_{[a] \cup [b, n]} + P_{[a+1] \cup [b, n-1]} P_{[a] \cup [b+1, n]}}{P_{[a] \cup [b, n-1]}} & \text{if $b-a \geq 4$} \\
		\frac{P_{[a+1] \cup [b+1, n-1]} P_{[a] \cup [b, n]} + \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-1]} \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-2] \backslash \{a+2\}} P_{[a] \cup [b+1, n]}}{P_{[a] \cup [b, n-1]}} & \text{if $b-a = 3$}
	\end{dcases*}
\] 
which is the same as \cref{eqn:minor-equation-1} except for the Pfaffians in the second case due to the parity condition in \cref{eqn:factorization-of-minor}. From the inductive hypothesis, we have the desired signs for minors of this form. Finally, we want to verify that 
\[
	\begin{cases}
		\text{$\operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n] \backslash \{i\}}) = (-1)^{i+1}$} \quad & \text{for $1 \leq i \leq n-2$} \\
		\text{$\operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-1] \cup \{n\}}) = -1$} \quad & \text{for $1 \leq k \leq m-1$} \\
		\text{$\operatorname{sign} (\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-2] \cup \{n\}}) = \operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n] \backslash \{n-1\}}) = -1$} \quad & \text{otherwise.}
	\end{cases}
\]
The last Pfaffian can be considered as a Pfaffian of the first type for $i = n-1$ and a Pfaffian of the second type for $k = m$. For this reason, we save the computation of its sign for last. 

The signs of $\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n] \backslash \{1\}}$ and $\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{1, n}$ are determined by the inductive hypothesis. For general $2 \leq i \leq n-2$, Corollary~\ref{cor:brill-theorem-extremal-case} gives us the relation  
	\begin{equation}
		\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n] \backslash \{i\}}  = \frac{P_{[i-2] \cup [i+1, n]} + \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n] \backslash \{i-1\}} \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-2] \backslash \{i\}}}{\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-2] \backslash \{i-1\}}}.
	\end{equation}
	This implies that we can induct on $i$ to prove $\operatorname{sign} (\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n] \backslash \{i\}}) = (-1)^{i+1}$, which is exactly what we wanted to show. For $2 \leq k \leq m-1$: 
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-1] \cup \{n\}} = \frac{P_{[2k-3] \cup \{n-1, n\}} + \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-1] \cup \{n-1\}} \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-3] \cup \{n\}}}{\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-3] \cup \{n-1\}}}. 
	\]
	From the inductive hypothesis, we get $\operatorname{sign} (\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[2k-1] \cup \{n\}}) = -1$ again by an inductive argument, which matches the claim. 
	
	The final sign we need to verify is $\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[1, n-2] \cup \{n\}}$. This comes from another relation of Corollary~\ref{cor:brill-theorem-extremal-case}
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[n-2] \cup \{n\}} = \frac{P_{[n-4] \cup \{n-1, n\}} + \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[1, n-1]} \operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[1, n-4] \cup \{n\}}}{\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[1, n-4] \cup \{n-1\}}}
	\]
	From the inductive hypothesis, we get $\operatorname{sign} (\operatorname{\mathbf{Pf}}_{[1, n-2] \cup \{n\}}) = -1$ which completes the induction.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
In the proof above, we technically only prove the equivalence between signed tests. However, the result as stated is still true. The relations which we use in the proof of \cref{thm:proof-of-positivity-test-matches-cluster-structure} are exactly the exchange relations of a mutation sequence which turns the initial seed of $\operatorname{Sk}_n$ to a seed which contains exactly the irreducible factors of the minors in~\cite{skew}. The mutations occur in exactly the same order in which we introduced the exchange relations. However, we could not find an enlightening proof of this fact other than a monstrous induction, which we omit.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- definition-22: body_md -->
\label{def:TP}\cite{Postnikov, Lusztig3}
The \emph{(totally) positive part} $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{>0}$
	of $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$ is the subset where all Pl\"ucker coordinates are strictly positive.  The \emph{totally nonnegative part} $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{\geq 0}$ of 
	$\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$ is the subset where all Pl\"ucker coordinates are nonnegative.
<!-- end definition-22 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
Since the set of Pl\"ucker coordinates are coordinates on
projective space, we could equivalently define the totally positive part of the 
Grassmannian by requiring that all Pl\"ucker coordinates have the same sign.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- definition-23: body_md -->
The \emph{positive grading} for $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$
is the grading \begin{equation} \label{eq:pos}
	\sigma^{+}: \mathcal{X} \to \{-1,1\} \hspace{.5cm} \text{ such that }
	\hspace{.5cm}
	\sigma^{+}(P_{I}) = 1 \text{ for all }I.
\end{equation}
	And the \emph{totally positive part} 
	$\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{>0}$ of the Grassmannian
	$\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$ is the subset 
$$\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{>0}:=\{C \ \vert \ \operatorname{sign}(P_{i_1,\dots,i_k}(C)) = 1.\}.$$
<!-- end definition-23 -->
<!-- definition-24: body_md -->
\label{def:alt}
	The \emph{alternating grading} for $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$
	is the grading \begin{equation} \label{eq:alt}
		\sigma^{\operatorname{alt}}: \mathcal{X} \to \{-1,1\} \hspace{.5cm} \text{ such that }
		\hspace{.5cm}
		\sigma^{\operatorname{alt}}(P_{i_1,\dots,i_k}) = (-1)^{i_1+ \dots + i_k}.
	\end{equation}
	And the \emph{alternating part} $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{\operatorname{alt}}$ of the Grassmannian $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$ is the subset 
	\[
		\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{\operatorname{alt}}:=\{C \ \vert \ \operatorname{sign}(P_{i_1,\dots,i_k}(C)) = (-1)^{i_1+\dots+i_k}\}.
	\]
<!-- end definition-24 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:alt1}
For any $V\in \operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$, the subspaces $V$
and $\operatorname{alt}(V^{\perp})\in \operatorname{Gr}_{n-k,n}$ have the same Pl\"ucker coordinates,
that is,
$$P_I(V) = P_{[n]\setminus I}(\operatorname{alt}(V^{\perp}))
	\hspace{.5cm}
	\text{ for all }I \in {[n] \choose k}.$$
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:alt2}
We have that 
\begin{equation}
	\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{\operatorname{alt}} = \{V^{\perp} \ \vert \ V\in \operatorname{Gr}_{n-k,n}^{>0} \},
\end{equation} that is, 
the alternating part $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{\operatorname{alt}}$ of the Grassmannian 
$\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$
is isomorphic to the totally positive part $\operatorname{Gr}_{n-k,n}^+$
of the Grassmannian $\operatorname{Gr}_{n-k,n}$ via the map 
$V \mapsto V^{\perp}$, where $V^{\perp}$ denotes
the orthogonal complement of $V$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Note that for $V\in \operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$ and $I=\{i_1,\dots,i_k\}$, 
we have $P_I(\operatorname{alt}(V)) = (-1)^{i_1+\dots+i_k} P_I(V)$.
	Using this observation together with \cref{lem:alt1}, it follows that
	 for $V\in \operatorname{Gr}_{n-k,n}^{>0}$,
	\begin{equation*}
		P_I(V^{\perp}) =(-1)^{i_1+\dots+i_k}P_I(\operatorname{alt}(V^{\perp})) = 
		(-1)^{i_1+\dots+i_k} P_{[n]\setminus I}(V) = 
		(-1)^{i_1+\dots+i_k}.
	\end{equation*}
	The result follows.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:posalt}
The gradings $\sigma^+$ and $\sigma^{\operatorname{alt}}$
come from signed seeds, and hence 
$\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{>0}$ and 
$\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{\operatorname{alt}}$ are homeomorphic to open balls.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
We can prove the first statement by verifying that  
\eqref{eq:grading2} holds, and using Pl\"ucker relations 
to deduce how the value of these gradings propagates away from the 
initial seed.
The fact that $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{>0}$ and 
$\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{\operatorname{alt}}$ are homeomorphic to open balls then follows from 
	\cref{thm:test}.   Note however that 
	it was already known from \cite{Postnikov} that $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{>0}$
	is homeomorphic to an open ball.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
By Mnev's Universality  Theorem~\cite{Mnev}, the topology of the 
realization space of an oriented matroid (that is, the 
subset of $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$ with a fixed sign pattern on Pl\"ucker coordinates) can be as complicated as that of any algebraic variety. 
However, it follows from \cref{thm:test} that any signed cell of 
$\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$ is homeomorphic to an open ball.  
Besides 
the totally positive part of $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$,
the alternating part of $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$
provides another nice subset with a fixed sign pattern which is 
topologically a ball.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
Sometimes it is more convenient to work with
 $\sigma^{\operatorname{alt}}(P_{I}) = (-1)^{i_1+ \dots + i_k+1}$ 
	instead of \eqref{eq:alt}.
This does not affect the corresponding (projectivized) signed cell of the Grassmannian, since Pl\"ucker coordinates are only defined up to a common scalar.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
Consider the Grassmannian $\operatorname{Gr}_{2,4}$ 
and the alternating grading $\sigma^{\operatorname{alt}}: \mathcal{X} \to \{-1,1\}$
defined by $\sigma^{\operatorname{alt}}(P_{ij}) = (-1)^{i+j+1}$.
Then $\operatorname{Gr}_{2,4}^{\operatorname{alt}}$ is the subset of $\operatorname{Gr}_{2,4}$
in which $P_{12}, P_{23}, P_{34},$ and $P_{14}$ are positive, while
$P_{13}$ and $P_{24}$ are negative.
More generally, $\operatorname{Gr}_{2,n}^{\operatorname{alt}}$ is the subset of 
$\operatorname{Gr}_{2,n}$ in which $P_{i,j}$ is positive if and only if 
$i+j$ is odd.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:G2nsigned}
Every signed cell of the Grassmannian $\operatorname{Gr}_{2,n}$ 
(with respect to the cluster structure described in \cref{sec:clusterGr}) is obtained from  the positive part of $\operatorname{Gr}_{2,n}$ via the torus action.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Consider an arbitrary signed cell $V^{\sigma}_{>0}$ of $\operatorname{Gr}_{2,n}$, 
	and let $C\in V^{\sigma}_{>0}$. 
If $t:=(t_1,\dots,t_n)$

is an element of the torus,  then 
$P_{ij}(t \cdot C) = t_i t_j P_{ij}(C)$.


Let $\{p_{ij}\ \vert \ 1 \leq i<j \leq n\} \in \{\pm 1\}^{n \choose 2}$
denote the signs of the Pl\"ucker coordinates of $C$.
We will find an element of the torus 
 $t:=(t_1,\dots,t_n)
\in \{\pm 1\}^n$  such that the Pl\"ucker coordinates
$P_{i, i+1}(t \cdot C)$ are positive for all $1 \leq i \leq n-1$.
To do so, let $t_1=1$, and  choose $t_2$ such that 
$p_{12}=t_1 t_2.$  Next we choose $t_3$ such that 
$p_{23} = t_2 t_3.$  We continue in this way, finally choosing $t_n$
such that $p_{n-1,n}=t_{n-1} t_n$.
Now we see that for $1 \leq i \leq n-1$, 
we get $\operatorname{sign}(P_{i,i+1}(t \cdot C)) = t_i t_{i+1} \operatorname{sign}(P_{i,i+1}(C)) = 
t_i t_{i+1} p_{i,i+1} =1$.


Our task is thus reduced to classifying the gradings
$\sigma=(\sigma_{ij})_{ij \in {[n] \choose 2}}$ from signed
seeds such that 
$\sigma_{i,i+1}>0$ for $1\leq i \leq n-1$.
Consider the rectangles seed for $\operatorname{Gr}_{2,n}$, shown for $n=9$ in 
\cref{fig:G29-quiver}.

Using 
\eqref{eq:grading2}
 and the fact that $\sigma_{i,i+1}>0$ for 
$1 \leq i \leq n-1$,  we see that  for $\operatorname{Gr}_{2,9}$,
we must have $\sigma_{79}=\sigma_{59}=\sigma_{39} = \sigma_{19}$
and $\sigma_{69}=\sigma_{49}=\sigma_{29}$.
More generally, we have $\sigma_{1n}=\sigma_{in}$ whenever $i$ is odd,
and $\sigma_{2n} = \sigma_{in}$ whenever $i$ is even.
Moreover, applying \eqref{eq:grading2} to the vertex labeled by 
the Pl\"ucker coordinate $P_{n-2,n}$, we see that 
$\sigma_{n-3,n}>0$.
It follows that  $\sigma_{in}=1$ when $i$ and $n$ have different parities.


This gives us the signs shown in  
\cref{fig:G29-quiver2}.

Finally we can either let $\sigma_{in}=1$ when $i$ and $n$ have the same parity, 
or we can let $\sigma_{in}=-1$ when $i$ and $n$ have the same parity.
Either choice
satisfies \eqref{eq:grading2} and hence gives a signed seed.
The first choice gives the totally positive part of $\operatorname{Gr}_{2,n}$,
and the second choice gives the alternating part.

<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:Gknsigned}
	Every signed cell of the Grassmannian $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$ (with respect to the cluster structure described in \cref{sec:clusterGr}) is obtained from the positive part $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$ via the torus action.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Consider an arbitrary signed cell $V^{\sigma}_{>0}$ of $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$, 
	and let $C\in V^{\sigma}_{>0}$. 
If $t:=(t_1,\dots,t_n)$ is an element of the torus, and $I=\{i_1<\dots < i_k\}$, then $P_{I}(t \cdot C) = t_{i_1} \dots t_{i_k} P_{I}(C)$.


We will prove \cref{thm:Gknsigned} by induction on $n$.  The base case
of $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,k+1}$ is trivial.
For the inductive step, we note that the seed for $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n-1}$ is 
a subseed for $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$: the quiver $Q_{k,n-1}$ and its Pl\"ucker coordinate labels
can be obtained from the corresponding quiver $Q_{k,n}$ by removing the rightmost 
column of vertices (and any incident arrows).
For example, the seed for $\operatorname{Gr}_{3,6}$ can be obtained from 
the seed for $\operatorname{Gr}_{3,7}$ shown in \cref{fig:G37-signed} by removing
the vertices labeled by $127, 167, 567$.
