Before proving the inductive step in general, we will illustrate it for our running
example in \cref{fig:G37-signed}.  Suppose that we know that the theorem is true for 
$\operatorname{Gr}_{3,6}$; we want to prove it for $\operatorname{Gr}_{3,7}$.
Consider an arbitrary signed cell $V_{3,7}^{\sigma}$
of $\operatorname{Gr}_{3,7}$ and the associated grading $\sigma$ on cluster variables.
This grading restricts to a grading on the cluster variables of $\operatorname{Gr}_{3,6}$ and gives a signed
cell $V_{3,6}^{\sigma}$ on $\operatorname{Gr}_{3,6}$.
Hence by the induction hypothesis
we can apply an element
of the torus $(t_1,\dots,t_6)\in \{-1,1\}^6$ such that the resulting signed cell $V_{3,6}^{\sigma'}$
is either the positive part  
or the alternating part of $\operatorname{Gr}_{3,6}$, as indicated by the signs labeling the 
$\operatorname{Gr}_{3,6}$ vertices at the left and right of 
\cref{fig:G37-signed}, respectively. Let $a,b,c\in\{-1,1\}$ be the resulting signs
on $127, 167, 567$.  The resulting sign pattern represents a signed seed
for $\operatorname{Gr}_{3,7}$, so in particular, 
\eqref{eq:grading2} holds.  


If $V_{3,6}^{\sigma'}$ is the positive part of 
$\operatorname{Gr}_{3,6}$, as in the left of \cref{fig:G37-signed}, then this ``balancing equation'' around vertex
$126$ implies that $a=b$, and the balancing equation around vertex $156$ implies that $b=c$. 
Thus $a=b=c$.  If $a=b=c=1$,  we set $t_7=1$, and if $a=b=c=-1$, we set $t_7=-1$.
It follows that acting on $V_{3,7}^{\sigma}$ by $(t_1,\dots,t_6,t_7)$ gives rise to the positive part
of $\operatorname{Gr}_{3,7}$.


Similarly, if $V_{3,6}^{\sigma'}$ is the alternating part of 
$\operatorname{Gr}_{3,6}$, as in the right of \cref{fig:G37-signed}, then the balancing equation around vertex
$126$ implies that $a=b$, and the balancing equation around vertex $156$ implies that $b=c$. 
Thus $a=b=c$.  If $a=b=c=1$,  we set $t_7=1$, and if $a=b=c=-1$, we set $t_7=-1$.
It follows that acting on $V_{3,7}^{\sigma}$ by $(t_1,\dots,t_6,t_7)$ gives rise to the alternating part
of $\operatorname{Gr}_{3,7}$.


The same argument works when we go from $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n-1}$ to $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$, but now we work with 
a more general quiver, as in 
\cref{fig:Gkn-signed}.

Here $u_1$, $v_1$, and $w_1$ represent the Pl\"ucker coordinates
$P_{1\dots k-1,n-2}$,
$P_{1\dots k-1,n-1}$, and
$P_{1\dots k-1,n}$; 
meanwhile $u_2$, $v_2$, and $w_2$ represent the Pl\"ucker coordinates
$P_{1\dots k-2,n-3,n-2}$,
$P_{1\dots k-2,n-2,n-1}$, and
$P_{1\dots k-2,n-1,n}$; etc.
If we start with an arbitrary signed cell $V^{\sigma}_{k,n}$ for $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$,
as before, it restricts to a signed cell for $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n-1}$, hence by the induction hypothesis
we can find a torus element $(t_1,\dots,t_{n-1})$ whose application produces a signed cell
$V^{\sigma'}_{k,n}$ whose restriction to $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n-1}$ is 
either: (1) the positive part or (2) the alternating part of 
 $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n-1}$.  Let $a_1,\dots,a_k$ be the remaining signs on the frozen variables $w_1,\dots,w_k$.


In Case (1), the balancing equation around $v_1, v_2,\dots,v_{k-1}$ implies $a_1=a_2=\cdots = a_k$. Since $w_1,\dots,w_k$ are the only Pl\"ucker coordinates labeling $Q_{k,n}$ involving the index $n$, we can choose an element $t_n$ that will ensure that these Pl\"ucker coordinates are positive. Thus, $(t_1,\dots,t_n) \cdot V^{\sigma}_{k,n}$ gives the positive part of $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$.


In Case (2), the balancing equation around $v_1$ implies that 
$$a_2 (-1)^{1+\dots + k-1 + (n-2)} = a_1 (-1)^{1+ \dots + k-2 + n-2 + n-1},$$ and hence
$a_2 = a_1 (-1)^{n-k}$. 
Meanwhile, the balancing equation around $v_2$ implies that 
$$a_3 (-1)^{1+ \dots + k-2+ (n-3)+(n-2)} (-1)^{1+ \dots + k-1+ (n-1)} = 
a_2 (-1)^{1+ \dots + k-3 + (n-2)+(n-2) + (n-1)} (-1)^{1+ \dots + k-1 + (n-2)},$$ which 
also implies that $a_3 = a_2 (-1)^{n-k}$.
In general, the balancing equation around $v_i$ implies that $a_{i+1} = a_i {(-1)}^{n-k}$
for $1 \leq i \leq k-1$,  which is exactly what we need to make sure that the signs
of $w_1, \ldots , w_k$ are consistent with the alternating part of $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}$.
Our last step is to choose $t_n = \pm 1$, in order to ensure that 
after we apply $(t_1,\ldots,t_n)$ to the original signed seed,
the sign of $w_1 = P_{1\cdots k-1,n}$ is correct, that is, $(-1)^{1+ \cdots + k-1 + n}$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:number-of-G-gradings-in-Gr}
	The cluster variety $\widehat{\operatorname{Gr}}_{k, n}$ has $|G|^n$ distinct $G$-gradings. These distinct $G$-gradings are determined by associating an element of $G$ to each vertex represented by the empty set, or a single row or a single column in the quiver shown in  the left diagram in~\cref{fig:G37-Le-quiver2}.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:frozen-leaf} and Lemma~\ref{lem:isolated-vertex} to the right hand side of the rectangles seed for $\widehat{\operatorname{Gr}}_{k, n}$ to reduce it to the rectangles seed for $\widehat{\operatorname{Gr}}_{k, n-1}$ and the result follows from induction.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:G-gradings-grassmannian}
	Let $G$ be a finite abelian group. Then $\widehat{\operatorname{Gr}}_{k, n}$ has $|G[k]|$ distinct $G$-gradings up to the torus action. When $G = \mathbb{Z} / p^m \mathbb{Z}$, distinct representatives of the $G$-gradings up to the torus action are given by the constant gradings $\sigma_x(P_I) := x$ for all $I \in \binom{[n]}{k}$ and $0 \leq x \leq p^{\min\{v_p(k), m\}}-1$.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
If we specialize to the case $p^m = 2$, then \cref{thm:G-gradings-grassmannian} implies that when $k$ is even, the cluster variety $\widehat{\operatorname{Gr}}_{k, n}$ has two signed seeds up to the torus action. When $k$ is odd, $\widehat{\operatorname{Gr}}_{k, n}$ has only one signed seed up to the torus action. In the even case, the distinct representatives are the \textit{totally positive grading} and the \textit{negative alternating grading} given by $\sigma(P_I) = (-1)^{i_1 + \ldots + i_k + 1}$. Note that when we descend this grading on $\operatorname{Gr}_{k, n}$, it is the same as the alternating grading.
<!-- end remark-17 -->
<!-- definition-25: body_md -->
A \emph{Le-diagram} for $\operatorname{Gr}_{k, n}$ is the data of a partition contained in a $k \times (n-k)$ rectangle with a filling of the boxes with dots, so that whenever a box is both below a dot and to the right of a dot, then it contains a dot. Equivalently, if we place the dots in the center of their corresponding boxes and draw downward and rightward rays from each dot (which we call the \textbf{hook} of that dot), then whenever two hooks intersect they must intersect at a dot. 
See \cref{fig:Le-diagram}.
<!-- end definition-25 -->
<!-- definition-26: body_md -->
Let $D$ be a Le-diagram. We construct a quiver $Q_D$ with vertices corresponding to the dots in $D$. It is convenient to identify the vertex corresponding to a dot with the region directly south-east of the dot. We say a region is \textbf{frozen} if it touches the boundary of the Young diagram. Otherwise, we call a region \textbf{mutable}. The frozen vertices in $Q_D$ are the vertices which correspond to frozen regions. Given this identification, we have the local rules shown in Figure~\ref{fig:local-rules} for constructing edges in the quiver\footnote{The stars in \cref{fig:local-rules} can either be mutable or frozen vertices. We only construct edges if the endpoints are not both frozen. The top left star might be the top left region which does not correspond to any dot. For the sake of the construction, we assume that this region is a vertex, and then delete this vertex afterwards.}. 

 	See~\cref{fig:quiver-of-Le-diagram} for a Le diagram with $7$ frozen regions, $4$ mutable regions, and also the associated quiver.
<!-- end definition-26 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
Let $Q_D$ be the quiver associated to a Le-diagram $D$ of 
	$\mathrm{Gr}_{k,n}$. Then the number of $G$-gradings on $\mathcal{A}(Q_D)$ is $|G|^{\# \text{frozen regions}}$.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
We describe an algorithm which simplifies a Le-diagram until it is empty and keeps track of the number of $G$-gradings. 

	\textbf{Step 0.} We first remove all rows with no dots. This changes both the bounding permutation and the placement of dots but it doesn't change the quiver. 

	\textbf{Step 1.} Consider the dot $\textbf{p}$ on the lowest row and furthest to the right. There cannot be any dots contained in boxes directly above the boxes directly to the right of $\textbf{p}$. Otherwise, the conditions of a Le-diagram would imply that there would be dots to the direct right of $\textbf{p}$. Thus, we can safely remove the boxes directly to the right of $\textbf{p}$ without changing the underlying quiver nor the number of $G$-gradings.

	\textbf{Step 2.} After \textit{Step 1}, we can assume that $\textbf{p}$ is contained in the last box on the last row. Now consider the part of the quiver local to $\textbf{p}$. There are four cases which are shown in Figure~\ref{fig:local-rules} where $\mathbf{p}$ is the bottom right vertex. In the first three situations, all three vertices are frozen and the vertex corresponding to $\textbf{p}$ is an isolated frozen vertex. Removing $\mathbf{p}$ from the Le-diagram and keeping the bounding partition is the same amounts to removing the corresponding frozen vertex on the quiver side. From Lemma~\ref{lem:isolated-vertex}, the number of $G$-gradings is $|G|$ times the number of $G$-gradings with $\mathbf{p}$ removed. \textit{In these three situations, the number of frozen regions decreases by $1$ and the number of mutable regions stays the same $1$}. In the fourth case, there are two subcases. Either all four vertices are frozen or all except the top left vertex is frozen. In both of these subcases, removing the dot $\mathbf{p}$ \textit{along with} the box from the bounding partition containing $\mathbf{p}$ amounts to removing the vertex corresponding to $\mathbf{p}$ from the quiver and freezing the top left vertex if it is not already frozen. If the top left vertex was originally not frozen, then Lemma~\ref{lem:frozen-leaf} implies that the number of $G$-gradings stays the same. \textit{In this situation, the number of frozen regions stay the same and the number of mutable regions decrease by $1$}. If the top left vertex was originally frozen, then the vertex of $\textbf{p}$ is an isolated frozen. Then, upon removal of $\textbf{p}$ and the box containing $\textbf{p}$, Lemma~\ref{lem:isolated-vertex} implies that the number of $G$-gradings get multiplied by $|G|$. \textit{In this situation, the number of frozen regions decreases by $1$ and the number of mutable regions stays the same.}

	Now, we keep repeating this process until the Le-diagram is empty. Throughout the process, the number of $G$-gradings is multiplied by $|G|$ exactly whenever the number of frozen regions decreases by $1$. Hence, the number of $G$-gradings is $|G|^{\# \text{frozen regions}}$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- definition-27: body_md -->
\label{defn_amplituhedron}
Fix $k, n, m$ positive integers such that $k+m \leq n$.
Let $Z\in \operatorname{Mat}_{n,k+m}^{>0}$. 
       The \emph{amplituhedron map}
$\tilde{Z}:\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{\ge 0} \to \operatorname{Gr}_{k,k+m}$
     is
      defined by
       $\tilde{Z}(C):=CZ$,
       where
 $C$ is a $k \times n$ matrix representing an element of
       $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{\ge 0}$,  and  $CZ$ is a $k \times (k+m)$ matrix representing an
         element of $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,k+m}$.
       The \emph{amplituhedron} $\mathcal{A}_{n,k,m}(Z) \subset \operatorname{Gr}_{k,k+m}$ is the image
$\tilde{Z}(\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{\ge 0})$
        inside $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,k+m}$.
<!-- end definition-27 -->
<!-- definition-28: body_md -->
\label{def:twistor}
       Choose
        $Z \in \operatorname{Mat}_{n,k+m}^{>0}$
        with rows  $Z_1,\dots, Z_n \in \mathbb{R}^{k+m}$.
        Given a matrix $Y$
        with rows $y_1,\dots,y_k$
        representing an element of $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,k+m}$,
        and $\{i_1,\dots, i_m\} \subset [n]$,
        we define the \emph{twistor coordinate}
        $\langle Y Z_{i_1} Z_{i_2} \cdots Z_{i_m} \rangle$
        to be  the determinant of the
        matrix with rows
        $y_1, \dots,y_k, Z_{i_1}, \dots, Z_{i_m}$.
        For $I=\{i_1<\dots <i_m\}$, we also
	use  $\langle Z_I(Y) \rangle$ to denote 
        $\langle Y Z_{i_1} Z_{i_2} \dots Z_{i_m} \rangle$.
<!-- end definition-28 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
Fix $n,k,m$ such that $k+m=n$, 
and choose
$Z \in \operatorname{Mat}_{n,k+m}^{>0}=\operatorname{Mat}_{n,n}^{>0}.$
The amplituhedron 
$\mathcal{A}_{n,k,m}(Z) = \mathcal{A}_{n,n-m,m}(Z)$
is the closure of the set
	$$\{Y \in \operatorname{Gr}_{k,k+m}=\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n} \ \vert \ 
\operatorname{sign} \langle Y Z_{i_1} \dots Z_{i_m} \rangle = (-1)^{i_1+ \dots + i_m +\delta} 
\text{ for all } 1 \leq i_1 < \dots < i_m \leq n\},$$
	where $\delta = mn + {m \choose 2}$ mod $2$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
The matrix $Z$ is invertible hence $\tilde{Z}$ is injective.
Moreover the amplituhedron can be written as
$\tilde{Z}(\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{\ge 0}) = \overline{\tilde{Z}(\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{>0})}$.
Choose $C\in \operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{>0}$, let $Y=CZ$, and choose $I=\{i_1< \dots < i_m\}$.
	It is not hard to check (see also \cite[(4.14)]{LKW})
	that  $$\langle Y Z_{i_1} \dots Z_{i_m} \rangle = 
	\langle Z_I(Y) \rangle=
	P_{[n]\setminus I}(C) \cdot \det(Z) (-1)^r,$$
	where $r$ is the number of swaps needed to 
put the sequence $1,2,\dots,\hat{i}_1, \dots, 
\hat{i}_m, \dots, n, i_1,\dots,i_m$ in increasing order.
In fact the number of swaps needed is 
$(n-i_1-(m-1))+(n-i_2-(m-2))+\dots+(n-i_m)$
which is congruent to $i_1+ \dots + i_m + mn+{m \choose 2}$
modulo $2$.
	Thus for all subsets $\{i_1 < \dots < i_m\} \subset [n]$ we have
 $$\langle Y Z_{i_1} \dots Z_{i_m} \rangle = 
	P_{[n]\setminus I}(C) \cdot \det(Z) (-1)^{i_1+ \dots + i_m+\delta}$$
	where $\delta = mn + {m \choose 2}$ mod $2$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- remark-18: body_md -->
Twistor coordinates can be identified with Pl\"ucker coordinates as follows, see \cite[Lemma 3.10 and Proposition 3.12]{karpwilliams}.
Fix $Z \in \operatorname{Mat}_{n,k+m}^{>0}$
and let
      $W\in \operatorname{Gr}_{k+m,n}^{>0}$
       be the column span of $Z$.
	Note that $\operatorname{Gr}_m(W) \subseteq Gr_{m,n}$.
        Define a map $f_Z: \operatorname{Gr}_m(W) \to \operatorname{Gr}_{k,k+m}$ by
       $$f_Z(X):= Z(X^{\perp}) = \{Z(x): x\in X^{\perp}\}.$$
        If we let $Y:=f_Z(X)$ then
        we have
        \begin{equation}\label{eq:identify}
		p_{I}(X) = \langle Z_{I}(Y) \rangle
                \qquad \text{ for all } \quad
                I \in {[n] \choose m}. 
        \end{equation}
<!-- end remark-18 -->
<!-- notation-1: body_md -->
Given a cluster variable $x$ in $\operatorname{Gr}_{m,n}$ (which is
	therefore a polynomial in Pl\"ucker coordinates) and 
	$Y\in \operatorname{Gr}_{k,k+m}$, we will denote
	by $x(Y)$ the polynomial in twistor coordinates obtained by 
	replacing each Pl\"ucker coordinate $p_I$ on $\operatorname{Gr}_{m,n}$
	by the corresponding twistor coordinate $\langle Z_I(Y) \rangle$
	on $\operatorname{Gr}_{k,k+m}$.  When it is clear from context, we will
	talk about cluster variables and the corresponding
	polynomials in twistor coordinates interchangeably.
<!-- end notation-1 -->
<!-- definition-29: body_md -->
\label{defn_tile}
	Fix $k, n, m$ with $k+m \leq n$ and choose
	$Z\in \operatorname{Mat}_{n,k+m}^{>0}$.  
	Given a positroid cell $S$ of 
	$\operatorname{Gr}_{k,n}^{\ge 0}$, we let 
	$Z_{S}^\circ := \tilde{Z}(S)$ and 
	$Z_{S}: = \overline{
		\tilde{Z}(S)} = \tilde{Z}(\overline{S})$.

	We call
	$Z_{S}$  and $Z_{S}^\circ$
	a \emph{tile}  and an \emph{open tile}
	for $\mathcal{A}_{n,k,m}$ 
	if $\dim(S) =km$ and 
	$\tilde{Z}$ is injective on $S$.
<!-- end definition-29 -->
<!-- conjecture-1: body_md -->
\label{conj:signed}
	Let $n,k,m$ be positive integers such that 
	$n \geq k+m$, and let $Z\in \operatorname{Mat}^{>0}_{n,k+m}$.
	Let $s=m(n-m)+1$, and 
	let $Z_{S}^\circ$ be an open tile for $\mathcal{A}_{n,k,m}(Z)$.
	There is a  seed  
	$(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}=(x_1,\dots,x_s),Q)$ for 
	$\operatorname{Gr}_{m,n}$ and signs $\sigma_i\in \{1,-1\}$ for each 
	$x_i\in \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}$ such that 
	\begin{equation*}
	Z_{S}^\circ=\{Y\in \operatorname{Gr}_{k,k+m}: \sigma_i \cdot x_i(Y) >0 \text{ for all }
		x_i\in \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}\}.
	\end{equation*}
Moreover, there is a subset $\mathbf{f} \subset \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}$ of \emph{facet variables} which are \emph{facets} of the tile
(see \cite[Definition 2.14]{ELPSTW}), and if we freeze these facet variables,
then the seed 
	$(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}},Q)$ together with the 
	signs $(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s)$ is a signed seed.
<!-- end conjecture-1 -->
<!-- definition-30: body_md -->
Consider an $n$-gon with boundary vertices labeled $1,\dots,n$ in clockwise
order.  We say that a \emph{diagonal} is a segment connecting
two boundary vertices.
	A \emph{bicolored subdivision} is a subdivision 
of the $n$-gon into polygons obtained by adding a collection of noncrossing
diagonals to the $n$-gon and coloring the resulting subpolygons 
black and white,
so that adjacent polygons have different colors.  A \emph{triangulated
	bicolored subdivision} $\mathcal{T}$ is a bicolored subdivision together with a 
triangulation of each black polygon (where the triangulation is 
obtained by adding some diagonals).
See \cref{fig:subdivision}. We say that the bicolored subdivision
	has \emph{type $(k,n)$} if a triangulation of it consists of 
	$k$ black triangles.
<!-- end definition-30 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\cite[Theorem 4.25 and Theorem 4.28]{PSW2}
The tiles for the amplituhedron $\mathcal{A}_{n,k,2}(Z)$
are in bijection with bicolored subdivisions
of type $(k,n)$.  Moreover, if $\mathcal{T}$
is a triangulated bicolored subdivision, then we have
that the corresponding tile is given by
\begin{equation*}
	Z_{S_{\mathcal{T}}}^\circ=\{Y\in \operatorname{Gr}_{k,k+2}: 
	(-1)^{\operatorname{area}(i\to j)} \langle Z_{ij}(Y) \rangle > 0 \text{ for all 
	black arcs }i \to j \text{ of }\mathcal{T} \text{ with }
	i<j\}.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:signed}
Given a triangulated bicolored subdivision of type 
$(k,n)$, we associate a quiver by placing a frozen node
on each boundary segment of a black polygon, and a mutable
node on each diagonal of a black polygon.  In each black triangle
we construct three arrows connecting the three nodes, oriented
clockwise
       as in \cref{fig:subdivision}
	(however as usual we can ignore arrows between
frozen nodes). The assignment ${(-1)}^{\operatorname{area}(i\to j)}$ of sign
to the node on the diagonal $i-j$ (where $i<j$) 
then gives this quiver
the structure of a signed seed.
In particular, \cref{conj:signed} holds for all tiles of the amplituhedron
$\mathcal{A}_{n,k,m}(Z)$ when $m=2$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
We need to show that at each mutable vertex, our assignment of signs
is balanced as in~\eqref{eq:grading2}. Suppose we have a mutable vertex at the diagonal
$i-k$, which lies inside a triangulated black quadrilateral on vertices $i<j<k<l$, see \cref{fig:verify}.

\begin{figure}
	\centering
    \resizebox{0.3\linewidth}{!}{
\begin{tikzpicture}
    \node[draw, circle, minimum size=2cm,
          inner sep=0pt, outer sep=0pt] (a) at (0,0) {};

    \foreach \direction in {north,east,south,west} {
        \fill (a.\direction) circle[radius=1pt];
    }
	\node[font = \tiny, xshift=0mm, yshift = 2mm] at (a.north) {$k$};
	\node[font = \tiny, xshift=2mm, yshift = 0mm] at (a.east) {$\ell$};
	\node[font = \tiny, xshift=-2mm, yshift = 0mm] at (a.west) {$j$};
	\node[font = \tiny, xshift=0mm, yshift = -2mm] at (a.south) {$i$};
	\draw (a.west) -- (a.north) -- (a.east) -- (a.south) -- cycle;
	\draw (a.north) -- (a.south);
	\node[font = \tiny] at ($1/3*(a.north) + 1/3*(a.west) + 1/3*(a.south)$) {$1$};
	\node[font = \tiny] at ($1/3*(a.north) + 1/3*(a.east) + 1/3*(a.south)$) {$1$};
	\node[font = \tiny, xshift = -1mm, yshift =1mm] at ($1/2*(a.north) + 1/2*(a.west)$) {$B$};
	\node[font = \tiny, xshift = 1mm, yshift =1mm] at ($1/2*(a.north) + 1/2*(a.east)$) {$C$};
	\node[font = \tiny, xshift = -1mm, yshift =-1mm] at ($1/2*(a.west) + 1/2*(a.south)$) {$A$};
	\node[font = \tiny, xshift = 1mm, yshift =-1mm] at ($1/2*(a.east) + 1/2*(a.south)$) {$D$};
\end{tikzpicture}
    }
	\caption{Verifying the signed seed property}\label{fig:verify}
\end{figure}

Let $A=\operatorname{area}(i\to j)$,$B=\operatorname{area}(j\to k)$, $C=\operatorname{area}(k\to l)$. To verify \eqref{eq:grading2}, we need to show that $\sigma(i-j) \sigma(k-l) = \sigma(j-k) \sigma(i-l)$, where $\sigma(i-j)$ denotes the sign (either $\pm 1$) associated to the diagonal $i-j$. Thus, we need to show that $\operatorname{area}(i\to j) + \operatorname{area}(k\to l)$ is congruent to $\operatorname{area}(j\to k) + \operatorname{area}(i\to l)$  modulo $2$, or equivalently $A+C$ is congruent to $B + (A+B+C+2)$.   This holds so we are done.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- definition-31: body_md -->
\cite[Definition 7.5]{RW}\label{def:tropmutation}
Let $\Sigma=(\tilde{B}, (x_1,\dots,x_s))$ be a seed and let 
$\Sigma':=\mu_k(\Sigma)$ be the seed obtained by mutation.
	We define the \emph{tropicalized  mutation  map} to be the map
$\Psi_{\Sigma, \Sigma'}: \mathbb{R}^s \to \mathbb{R}^s$ defined by 
\[(\sigma_1,\dots, \sigma_s) \mapsto
	(\sigma_1,\dots, \sigma_{k-1}, \sigma'_k, \sigma_{k+1},\dots, \sigma_s),\] where
\[
	\sigma'_k := \min \left( \sum_{b_{ik}>0} b_{ik} \sigma_i,\sum_{b_{ik}<0} -b_{ik} \sigma_i \right) - \sigma_k.
\]
<!-- end definition-31 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:tropmutation}\cite[Lemma 7.12]{RW2}
	We use the notation of \cref{def:tropmutation}. Suppose that $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s)$ and $\tau=(\tau_1,\dots,\tau_s)$ lie in $\mathbb{R}^s$, and $(\tilde{B},\sigma)$ is $\mathbb{R}$-balanced. Then the tropicalized mutation map is linear at $\sigma$: that is, we have 
	\[
		\Psi_{\Sigma,\Sigma'}(\sigma+\tau)=\Psi_{\Sigma,\Sigma'}(\sigma)+\Psi_{\Sigma,\Sigma'}(\tau).
	\]
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- definition-32: body_md -->
\label{Xseed}
	Let $\tilde{B}$ be an $s \times r$ exchange matrix and let $(y_1,\dots,y_s)$ be a set of parameters. For $1 \leq k \leq r$, we define a new set of parameters $(y'_1,\dots,y'_s)$ where
	\begin{equation}\label{e:XclusterMut}
		y'_{i} = \begin{cases}
			\frac{1}{y_{k}} & \text{if }i = k, \\
			y_{i}(1+y_{k})^{b_{i k}} & \text{if }b_{i k}\geq 0 \text{ and }i\neq k,\\
			{y_{i}}(1+y_{k}^{-1})^{b_{i k}} & \text{if }b_{i k}\leq 0 \text{ and }i \neq k
		\end{cases}
	\end{equation}
	We say that $(\mu_{k}(\tilde B), (y'_1,\dots,y'_s))$ is obtained from $(\tilde B, (y_1,\dots,y_s))$ by \emph{$Y$-seed mutation} in direction $k$, and we refer to the ordered pairs $(\mu_{k}(\tilde B), (y'_1,\dots,y'_s))$  and $(\tilde B, (y_1,\dots,y_s))$ as \emph{labeled $Y$-seeds}. If $f$ is a rational expression in the parameters $(y_1,\dots,y_s)$, we use $\operatorname{Mut}_{Y,k}(f)$ to denote the new expression for $f$ obtained by rewriting it in terms of   $(y'_1,\dots,y'_s)$.
<!-- end definition-32 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{l:monomialXmutation}~\cite[Lemma 15.9]{RW}
	Let $(\tilde B, (y_1,\dots,y_s))$ be a {labeled ${Y}$-seed} as above, and let $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s)\in\mathbb{Z}^s$. Let $y^{\sigma}:=y_1^{\sigma_1} \dots y_s^{\sigma_s}$ be the corresponding Laurent monomial in $y_1 \dots y_s$. Choose $1 \leq k \leq r$. Then the $Y$-seed mutation $\operatorname{Mut}_{Y,k}(y^{\sigma})$ of $y^{\sigma}$ is a Laurent monomial in $y'_1 \dots y'_s$ if and only if $(\tilde B, (\sigma_1,\dots, \sigma_s))$ is $\mathbb{Z}$-balanced at $k$. Moreover, in that case, $\operatorname{Mut}_{Y,k}(y^{\sigma})$ is a Laurent monomial with new exponent vector $(\sigma'_1,\dots, \sigma'_s)\in \mathbb{Z}^s$ given by 

	\begin{equation}\label{e:balancedMutation}
		\sigma'_j=
			\begin{cases}
				(\sum_{b_{ik}>0} b_{ik} \sigma_i) - \sigma_k, & j=k,\\
				\sigma_j, & j \ne k.
			\end{cases}
	\end{equation}
	Note that since $(\tilde B, \sigma)$ is $\mathbb{Z}$-balanced at vertex $k$, this is an instance of tropicalized  mutation.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
Let $(\tilde B, (y_1,\dots,y_s))$ be a {labeled ${Y}$-seed}, and let $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_s)\in\mathbb{Z}^s$. If $(\tilde B, (\sigma_1,\dots, \sigma_s))$ is $\mathbb{Z}$-balanced (at all vertices), then $y^{\sigma}$ is regular on the corresponding cluster variety.\footnote{A regular function that looks like an ordinary Laurent monomial in at least one cluster chart is also called a \emph{global monomial}.}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
